=================== case-study--joe-thomas-win-rate-versus-sacks-allowed.md
confidence: untested

# Case Study: Joe Thomas, Pass Block Win Rate and the Quarterback Who Held the Ball

**What it is** — Panelists describe how ESPN's pass block and pass rush win rates came about accidentally: a script written to find the closest defender on each pass, to answer researchers' repeated questions about separation, drew a visualization that showed who was blocking whom (teg9SfzpMy0 [14:59], [15:30]). From there a pass block win rate was "a short step": if you can get your shoulder pads past the block it is a pass rush win, with a time component (teg9SfzpMy0 [15:30]). The first check: Joe Thomas, in his final season (2017), was about 53rd in sacks allowed or pressures allowed (the speaker is unsure which) but third in pass block win rate (teg9SfzpMy0 [16:02]). A panelist's first reaction was "our metric is broken." On film Thomas was doing as well as he always had; his quarterback (caption "DeSean Kaiser") held the ball for about seven seconds and then got sacked, and "you can't expect any alignment to sustain a block that long" (teg9SfzpMy0 [16:34]). They conclude the conventional line metrics (pressures and sacks allowed) did not tell the whole story (teg9SfzpMy0 [14:29]).

**Why it works** — A panelist's reading of the Thomas case: he was doing his job as well as always, and the quarterback held the ball for about seven seconds before the sack (teg9SfzpMy0 [16:34]). A panelist describes win rate as the percent of time a player can sustain a block or beat a block by 2.5 seconds (teg9SfzpMy0 [41:43]). Inference: sacks allowed also depend on how long the quarterback holds the ball, which win rate does not, and a metric that attributes an outcome to the wrong player will look wrong against a player known to be good, and film can show why.

**When to apply** — As the sanity-check pattern for a new metric: compare it with players whose quality is already well known, then watch the surprising cases. Eric's baseline: "There is a place for the coach's eye: when something looks off, it can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q6). Inference: here the direction runs the other way, film questioning a metric, which supports the same sequence of observation and checking.

**When NOT to apply** — One player and one season, told as a story, with no group-level comparison (teg9SfzpMy0 [16:02]). `untested`. The speaker is unsure whether the comparison metric was sacks or pressures allowed. Names are caption spellings. The panel notes the story was also "a really good story line" that helped sell the metric to ESPN colleagues, so it is a persuasion case as well as a check (teg9SfzpMy0 [16:02], [17:35]). A single clean explanation does not validate a metric.

**Example** — A panelist's, above (Thomas, third in win rate, about 53rd in the older metric).

**Related** — [[claim--expected-pressure-rate-adds-to-pressure-rate-in-predicting-sacks]], the SSAC22 talk's pressure-versus-sack framing, a similar process measure; [[heuristic--year-to-year-stability-as-test-of-real-skill]].
=================== claim--quarterback-and-scheme-entangle-with-receiver-open-score.md
confidence: untested

# Quarterback and Scheme Are Entangled With a Receiver's Open Score

**What it is** — A panelist says the team had assumed the quarterback would matter for catch score and less for YAC, while getting open would belong to the receiver, the play design and the opponent, "but what we found is that's not true" (teg9SfzpMy0 [29:25], [29:55]). To account for it they ran an adjusted plus-minus of quarterbacks and receivers across multiple seasons, using a good mix of pairings (teg9SfzpMy0 [29:55]). Their finding: quarterbacks consistently help receivers get a better open score for reasons the panel can only list (target choice, extending plays, reading the field, possibly looking off safeties). The example: Patrick Mahomes was "pretty average" on catch score once his throws were accounted for, but "blows it out of the water" on open score (teg9SfzpMy0 [30:27], [30:57]). In Q&A, scheme and quarterback cannot be separated: quarterbacks stay in one scheme and the data do not allow a controlled experiment such as moving Mahomes to a different system; the model includes route and coverage context, a "sliver" of scheme, and no overall team or coach variable (teg9SfzpMy0 [51:25], [51:55], [52:25], [52:56]).

A hedged application: Seattle's receivers rated near the top with or without Russell Wilson and Denver's were last, so part of Wilson's decline could lie with the receivers; the panel says it is not claiming Wilson's decline is not his (teg9SfzpMy0 [33:59], [34:32], [35:02]).

**Why it works** — The panel's account is that the quarterback's choices change which receivers are open (teg9SfzpMy0 [30:27], [30:57]). They say they cannot tell which of those it is. Inference: any receiver number is a receiver-plus-quarterback-plus-scheme number until the three can be separated by pairings or changes of team.

**When to apply** — As a standing caveat on receiver (and similar) metrics, and a reason to compare players who changed teams. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12): ACWR is "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally" (Explicit). Inference: both warn against reading a context-free number as a player trait.

**When NOT to apply** — The panel gives no size for the quarterback effect and no adjusted values in the captions. `untested`. The Wilson story is explicitly speculative, and the panel's own wording is "maybe there's more to the story" (teg9SfzpMy0 [35:02], [35:32]). NFL tracking data with x and y only. Not applicable to college data without a similar tracking source.

**Example** — The panel's: Mahomes, average on catch score but very high on open score (teg9SfzpMy0 [30:27]).

**Related** — [[claim--scheme-confound-is-only-partly-handled-by-propensity-weighting]], the SSAC26 talk reaches the scheme limit on the defensive side (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43], [12:43]); [[framework--open-score-orientation-speed-trajectory-before-release]]; [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]].
=================== framework--open-score-orientation-speed-trajectory-before-release.md
confidence: untested

# Open Score: Orientation, Speed and Trajectory Measured Before Release, Not Separation

**What it is** — ESPN's receiver tracking metrics (RTM) have three parts: open score, catch score and yards-after-catch (YAC) score (teg9SfzpMy0 [04:06]). Panelists (the host introduces Seth Walder, Brian Burke and Allison Labs, caption spelling; the auto-captions do not label who speaks) describe open score as how open a receiver gets, and say it is not just the distance to the closest defender (teg9SfzpMy0 [06:12], [06:45]). The model uses x-y tracking positions plus more:
- **Orientation:** in a slant on fourth and four, the defender is within about a yard and a half at ball arrival, but the receiver faces where the ball is going and the defender is out of position, so the model scores him open (teg9SfzpMy0 [05:41], [06:12]).
- **Speed and trajectory:** on a play where the receiver looks open in a still frame, he is going 9 mph and the defender 13 mph, and the defender is coming faster and undercuts the route; the model scores him not open and the pass is broken up (teg9SfzpMy0 [09:21], [09:51]). On a hitch, the receiver is going 4.6 mph and the defender 10.3, and the model anticipates separation (teg9SfzpMy0 [07:47], [08:19]).
- **Untargeted receivers get credit:** the question asked of the receiver is only whether he got open (teg9SfzpMy0 [07:16], [07:47]).
- **Timing:** the model looks at 0.2 seconds before pass release, because in zone coverage defenders collapse on the target and leave untargeted receivers open (teg9SfzpMy0 [08:19], [08:50]).
- **Gravity:** extra credit when a receiver draws multiple defenders within a threshold (teg9SfzpMy0 [47:18], [47:49]).

**Why it works** — The panelists' reasoning is that open is "a different thing" from separation and a model that only used the straight-line distance would mislabel both cases above (teg9SfzpMy0 [06:12], [06:45]). The captions give no model internals for open score. A panelist says the whole system uses a position-invariant convolutional neural network for catch probability (teg9SfzpMy0 [23:47]); whether open score uses the same network is not said. Inference: a measure built from positions, directions and speeds can separate a receiver who looks open from one who is open.

**When to apply** — When a single distance or "separation" number is being used as the measure of an athlete's success. Eric's baseline: force plate reporting follows an output, driver and strategy framework (adopted practice, the framework is Hawkin Dynamics' own), with extra metrics added "only with a specific, defensible rationale." Inference: the lesson here is similar, not identical: a single output value (distance) hides the drivers (orientation, speed, trajectory).

**When NOT to apply** — Illustrated with a handful of clips, mostly one receiver (AJ Brown), and no numbers on accuracy in the captions. `untested`. The data are NFL tracking data with x and y only, no z-axis (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:15]), no game-leverage context (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:46], [47:18]) and no quarterback progression (teg9SfzpMy0 [45:15]). A panelist says the right timing might be a fraction of a second before or after 0.2 seconds, and that is unknown without the progression data (teg9SfzpMy0 [45:45]). The stated purpose is fan content, not team use (teg9SfzpMy0 [02:03]).

**Example** — The panel's: AJ Brown scores highest in the league midseason, an overall 86, five points above the next player (the captions give "Travis Kelsey," a caption spelling) (teg9SfzpMy0 [03:05]).

**Related** — [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]], [[heuristic--year-to-year-stability-as-test-of-real-skill]], [[case-study--speed-adjusted-receiver-grade-landry-kupp-brown]].
=================== framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates.md
confidence: untested

# When the Athlete Creates His Own Context: Combine General and Specific Context Estimates

**What it is** — In catch score, a panelist describes a "catch over predicted" residual: the model predicts a catch probability, and the receiver is credited the remainder if he catches it and debited the predicted probability if not (a 0.75 prediction and a catch is credited +0.25) (teg9SfzpMy0 [24:17], [24:48]). The problem that "almost killed" the project: the receiver creates the context himself (the move that got him open), so a model that adjusts for the field at ball arrival penalizes him for making the catch easy (teg9SfzpMy0 [24:48], [25:18]). The solution, described as a "Eureka moment":
- **General context ("expected" in their words):** coverage, route, depth, play action, slot alignment and distance from the sideline (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:49], [26:20]).
- **Specific context ("predicted"):** all the tracking positions at ball arrival, through a position-invariant convolutional neural network (teg9SfzpMy0 [23:47], [26:20]).
- **Combination:** both helped predict yards per route run, so catch score combines the two (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]).
- Without the combination, contested-catch receivers would benefit from their inability to create separation (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52], [27:22]). The panel says completion probability over expected for quarterbacks cannot be turned around for receivers for the same reason (teg9SfzpMy0 [27:52], [28:23]).

**Why it works** — The panelist's account is only that the general context removes the problem of the receiver generating his own context, and that both estimates helped predict yards per route run (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:20], [26:52]). Inference: the general estimate does not see the receiver's separation and the specific estimate does, so the pair brackets how hard the catch was relative to how he got there. The panel gives no test showing that the combination removes the bias. Inference: the combination is a compromise, justified by predicting yards per route run (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]), not by showing context was removed.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's own action changes the conditions of the thing being graded. Inference: in a jump or sprint assessment, an athlete who changes his own start or setup alters the test condition, so the comparison should hold the conditions that he controls fixed, or be labeled.

**When NOT to apply** — The captions give no quantities for either estimate or for the combined catch score, and the check against yards per route run is qualitative (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]). `untested`. The data are NFL tracking data, x and y only (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:15]). A panelist adds YAC uses video-tracked ball placement as well as the dots (teg9SfzpMy0 [28:55]), so video charting is also part of the system. The metric is for fan content.

**Example** — The panel's: Alan Robinson, Kenny Golladay and Terry McLaurin (caption spellings) as contested-catch receivers who would look best if the context credit weren't adjusted (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52], [27:22]).

**Related** — [[principle--prediction-is-not-attribution-in-defensive-evaluation]], the SSAC26 talk's version of the credit problem for defenders; [[heuristic--build-a-simple-benchmark-model-beside-the-complex-one]]; [[framework--open-score-orientation-speed-trajectory-before-release]]; [[claim--quarterback-and-scheme-entangle-with-receiver-open-score]].
=================== framework--weight-mixed-unit-components-by-correlation-with-an-outcome.md
confidence: untested

# Weight Mixed-Unit Components by Their Correlation With an Accepted Outcome

**What it is** — The overall receiver score combines open, catch and YAC components with different units: YAC is in yards above expected, the others are residual catch-probability style quantities, so there is a "unit mismatch" (teg9SfzpMy0 [36:32]). The panel's solution:
- **Weights differ by position:** receivers and tight ends are slightly different, running backs very different (teg9SfzpMy0 [36:02], [36:32]).
- **Target outcome:** yards per route run, described as probably the best conventional statistic for grading a receiver's season (teg9SfzpMy0 [37:03]).

# Open Score: Orientation, Speed and Trajectory Measured Before Release, Not Separation

**What it is** — ESPN's receiver tracking metrics (RTM) have three parts: open score, catch score and yards-after-catch (YAC) score (teg9SfzpMy0 [04:06]). Panelists (the host introduces Seth Walder, Brian Burke and Allison Labs, caption spelling; the auto-captions do not label who speaks) describe open score as how open a receiver gets, and say it is not just the distance to the closest defender (teg9SfzpMy0 [06:12], [06:45]). The model uses x-y tracking positions plus more:
- **Orientation:** in a slant on fourth and four, the defender is within about a yard and a half at ball arrival, but the receiver faces where the ball is going and the defender is out of position, so the model scores him open (teg9SfzpMy0 [05:41], [06:12]).
- **Speed and trajectory:** on a play where the receiver looks open in a still frame, he is going 9 mph and the defender 13 mph, and the defender is coming faster and undercuts the route; the model scores him not open and the pass is broken up (teg9SfzpMy0 [09:21], [09:51]). On a hitch, the receiver is going 4.6 mph and the defender 10.3, and the model anticipates separation (teg9SfzpMy0 [07:47], [08:19]).
- **Untargeted receivers get credit:** the question asked of the receiver is only whether he got open (teg9SfzpMy0 [07:16], [07:47]).
- **Timing:** the model looks at 0.2 seconds before pass release, because in zone coverage defenders collapse on the target and leave untargeted receivers open (teg9SfzpMy0 [08:19], [08:50]).
- **Gravity:** extra credit when a receiver draws multiple defenders within a threshold (teg9SfzpMy0 [47:18], [47:49]).

**Why it works** — The panelists' reasoning is that open is "a different thing" from separation and a model that only used the straight-line distance would mislabel both cases above (teg9SfzpMy0 [06:12], [06:45]). The captions give no model internals for open score. A panelist says the whole system uses a position-invariant convolutional neural network for catch probability (teg9SfzpMy0 [23:47]); whether open score uses the same network is not said. Inference: a measure built from positions, directions and speeds can separate a receiver who looks open from one who is open.

**When to apply** — When a single distance or "separation" number is being used as the measure of an athlete's success. Eric's baseline: force plate reporting follows an output, driver and strategy framework (adopted practice, the framework is Hawkin Dynamics' own), with extra metrics added "only with a specific, defensible rationale." Inference: the lesson here is similar, not identical: a single output value (distance) hides the drivers (orientation, speed, trajectory).

**When NOT to apply** — Illustrated with a handful of clips, mostly one receiver (AJ Brown), and no numbers on accuracy in the captions. `untested`. The data are NFL tracking data with x and y only, no z-axis (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:15]), no game-leverage context (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:46], [47:18]) and no quarterback progression (teg9SfzpMy0 [45:15]). A panelist says the right timing might be a fraction of a second before or after 0.2 seconds, and that is unknown without the progression data (teg9SfzpMy0 [45:45]). The stated purpose is fan content, not team use (teg9SfzpMy0 [02:03]).

**Example** — The panel's: AJ Brown scores highest in the league midseason, an overall 86, five points above the next player (the captions give "Travis Kelsey," a caption spelling) (teg9SfzpMy0 [03:05]).

# When the Athlete Creates His Own Context: Combine General and Specific Context Estimates

**What it is** — In catch score, a panelist describes a "catch over predicted" residual: the model predicts a catch probability, and the receiver is credited the remainder if he catches it and debited the predicted probability if not (a 0.75 prediction and a catch is credited +0.25) (teg9SfzpMy0 [24:17], [24:48]). The problem that "almost killed" the project: the receiver creates the context himself (the move that got him open), so a model that adjusts for the field at ball arrival penalizes him for making the catch easy (teg9SfzpMy0 [24:48], [25:18]). The solution, described as a "Eureka moment":
- **General context ("expected" in their words):** coverage, route, depth, play action, slot alignment and distance from the sideline (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:49], [26:20]).
- **Specific context ("predicted"):** all the tracking positions at ball arrival, through a position-invariant convolutional neural network (teg9SfzpMy0 [23:47], [26:20]).
- **Combination:** both helped predict yards per route run, so catch score combines the two (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]).
- Without the combination, contested-catch receivers would benefit from their inability to create separation (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52], [27:22]). The panel says completion probability over expected for quarterbacks cannot be turned around for receivers for the same reason (teg9SfzpMy0 [27:52], [28:23]).

**Why it works** — The panelist's account is only that the general context removes the problem of the receiver generating his own context, and that both estimates helped predict yards per route run (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:20], [26:52]). Inference: the general estimate does not see the receiver's separation and the specific estimate does, so the pair brackets how hard the catch was relative to how he got there. The panel gives no test showing that the combination removes the bias. Inference: the combination is a compromise, justified by predicting yards per route run (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]), not by showing context was removed.

**When to apply** — When an athlete's own action changes the conditions of the thing being graded. Inference: in a jump or sprint assessment, an athlete who changes his own start or setup alters the test condition, so the comparison should hold the conditions that he controls fixed, or be labeled.

**When NOT to apply** — The captions give no quantities for either estimate or for the combined catch score, and the check against yards per route run is qualitative (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52]). `untested`. The data are NFL tracking data, x and y only (teg9SfzpMy0 [46:15]). A panelist adds YAC uses video-tracked ball placement as well as the dots (teg9SfzpMy0 [28:55]), so video charting is also part of the system. The metric is for fan content.

**Example** — The panel's: Alan Robinson, Kenny Golladay and Terry McLaurin (caption spellings) as contested-catch receivers who would look best if the context credit weren't adjusted (teg9SfzpMy0 [26:52], [27:22]).

**Why it works** — The panel's reasoning is audience fit: fans are "kind of checked out" by z-scores, and a name implying a verdict claims more than the number delivers (teg9SfzpMy0 [41:43], [42:14]). They give no test of the choice. Inference: a plain-language definition lets a reader see what the number can and cannot say.

**When to apply** — Whenever a number goes to coaches or athletes. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q28): coach-facing reports are built by strength staff for most teams, and sport science staff provide them when applicable (Explicit). Inference: the person building the report picks the label, so name the number for what it counts ("percent of reps above a speed threshold"), not as a grade.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a communication practice from a media organization whose stated aim is to "engage and entertain the fans," not to help a team win (teg9SfzpMy0 [02:03]). `untested`. # Test a New Metric by Whether It Travels With the Player From Year to Year

**What it is** — A panelist states the check: "you examine the correlation of a metric from year to year at the player level." If the metric measures something systematic about talent or production, it will correlate and travel with the player from year to year and from team to team (teg9SfzpMy0 [54:29]). Their result: open score is the most stable of the three receiver components, "about as consistent as batting averages" in baseball (teg9SfzpMy0 [54:59]). The order of the other two is garbled: first stated as open, then catch, then YAC, then a moment of back-and-forth ("other way around"... "I think I was right the first time") leaves it unclear (teg9SfzpMy0 [53:28], [54:59]). The panel is explicit that this is stability (the metric predicting itself), not predictiveness of yards per route run or receiving yards, which is "TBD" (teg9SfzpMy0 [53:28], [53:59]). For the earlier pass-block and pass-rush win rates, they say players hold the skill from year to year, and a pass rusher's win rate within two and a half seconds indicates future sack ability, with a separate finishing skill (teg9SfzpMy0 [55:29], [57:00]). In a different talk, Eric Eager says his bite-distance trait is about three or four times more predictive year to year (by R-squared) than the coverage grade (Q3i3FOC-dPE [11:53], [12:23]).

**Why it works** — The panelists' rationale: a stable correlation means the metric picks up something systematic, not noise (teg9SfzpMy0 [54:29]). Inference: stability alone does not show validity; a steady measure of the wrong thing is still wrong.

**When to apply** — Before a number goes into a coach-facing report. Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, SportSmith 2026-02-20). Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a) uses "standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" (Explicit). Inference: a year-to-year or block-to-block correlation is a player-level check that sits beside those, for talent assessment; volatile measures are better suited for day-to-day monitoring only.

**When NOT to apply** — No correlation values are given in the captions, only the batting-average comparison, and the panelists disagreed about the order in the captions (teg9SfzpMy0 [54:59]). `untested`. Stability across seasons depends on quarterback and scheme (see [[claim--quarterback-and-scheme-entangle-with-receiver-open-score]]). With short careers or few reps per season the check cannot be run (the panel does not say what sample was used).

**Example** — The panelist's: open score near the stability of batting average (teg9SfzpMy0 [54:59]).

confidence: untested

# The Pressure Score Is Validated Only by Proxy and Does Not Assign Pressure to a Player

**What it is** — Three limits the speaker states or concedes in the talk and Q&A.

1. **Proxy evaluation only.** A continuous score is "hard to evaluate", so accuracy is measured through the maximum pressure on a passer compared with PFF hurry, hit and sack labels (1nt8hK2oYrE [10:54], [11:26]). No accuracy figure for the final score appears in the captions (the caption "Fon score of the 0.99 for the identification and also the close 0.91 for the matchup", read here as F1, belongs to the earlier identification and matchup stages, 1nt8hK2oYrE [07:47]).
2. **No player-level disentangling.** Asked how the model disentangles which player produced the pressure, the speaker answers "we didn't actually try to disentangle which pressure is coming from which specific player" (1nt8hK2oYrE [21:40]); the target is "forgiving" and credits rushers inside a threshold area (1nt8hK2oYrE [22:12]), and the speaker says they did not want to treat individual scores as each player's contribution to the whole (the caption is garbled: "didn't want to calculate the pressure individual players pressure score as the contribution of the this defensive Play", 1nt8hK2oYrE [22:43]).
3. **No validation against a correlate.** Asked whether the score was checked against quarterback motion, the speaker says no correlation analysis was done, and points to relative position, velocity and acceleration features instead (1nt8hK2oYrE [23:13], [23:43]).

**Talk's own tension.** The sample plays credit individual players with high pressure scores (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00], [14:04]) while the Q&A says the model does not separate whose pressure it is. The talk does not reconcile these. The summary file for this talk reads it the same way.

Also named: scheme and strategy not modeled (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]), and complex position features not modeled (1nt8hK2oYrE [18:38]).

**Why it works** — Not applicable; this is a limits entry. The speaker gives no mechanism for the performance disparity the speaker mentions (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:58]).

**When to apply** — As a checklist of what to ask a vendor or analyst who offers a "pressure" or "pressure rate" metric: how is the continuous score validated, does it assign credit to an individual, and what independent variable was it checked against. Inference: ask the same of any per-player number.

Eric's baseline: "I think it's raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q12, about ACWR; Explicit.) Inference: a number validated only by proxy, with credit not tied to a person, deserves the same caution before it enters a decision.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the speaker's account of one NFL-based framework (public Big Data Bowl data with PFF labels). It says nothing about other pressure models, and the captions around the accuracy statement are garbled (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:26], [11:58]), so an actual accuracy figure may have been stated and lost. Marked untested because no result with a number backs the score itself.

**Example** — The Q&A exchange itself (1nt8hK2oYrE [21:09], [21:40]).

**Related** — [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]; [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]]; [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]].

confidence: untested

# Pressure Score: A Blocker-Interference Feature and a Forgiving Label

**What it is** — Stage 3 of Hong's pipeline (see [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]]) models pressure as a probability that a rusher gets a hit, hurry or sack, on a 0 to 1 scale "at any point in time during the play" (1nt8hK2oYrE [08:47], [09:19]). Two design choices are the useful part.

**1. A blocker-interference feature.** For each rusher, an "area of interest" is set by distance and angle between the rusher and the passer, and the number of blockers inside it is counted, to measure the resistance the rusher may meet (1nt8hK2oYrE [09:51], [10:23]). It sits alongside the static and dynamic tracking features from the matchup stage and relative position, velocity and acceleration to the passer (1nt8hK2oYrE [09:51], [23:43]).

**2. A forgiving target.** Targets are the manually labeled PFF hurry, hit and sack, plus an engineered label based on the rusher's distance to the passer at a point in time (1nt8hK2oYrE [10:23], [10:54]). In Q&A he describes it as one rusher getting within one yard of the passer before one second; the captions are garbled, so the exact rule is uncertain (1nt8hK2oYrE [20:39]). The reason he gives: "it is not always the one player gets a sack", so a rusher who gets into the threshold area earns credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [22:12]).

Main drivers he gives (a light feature analysis, no values stated): the rusher's relative position to the passer, velocity and acceleration, initial position (who starts close), and how many blockers the rusher faces, with an open rusher more likely to generate pressure (1nt8hK2oYrE [17:37], [18:08], [18:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the intent (credit more than the sack-taker) but no test of the engineered label. Inference: a distance-based label turns a rare event (sack) into a more frequent one, which gives a model more signal to learn from.

**When to apply** — When an event label is rare and a process variable (distance, time) is available: consider a second, softer label, and disclose how it was set. Count obstructions between a mover and a target as a feature when tracking is available.

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-20). Inference: label consistency is the weakest point here; PFF hurry and hit labels are subjective hand labels, and the engineered label rule is not fully stated in the talk.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested. The speaker reports "great accuracy" against PFF labels and better calibration (expected and maximum calibration error) for the random forest, with no values (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:26] to [12:28]). No accuracy figure, no feature weights, no validation of the engineered label. The model "didn't actively account for" complex position features (1nt8hK2oYrE [18:38]), and team scheme and strategies are left as future work (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). It was trained on NFL data and PFF labels. The speaker did not check correlation with quarterback motion (1nt8hK2oYrE [23:13]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a passer forced toward the sideline after heavy pressure (caption wording: "forced... to be out of the... sideline", garbled), where the model credits two rushers (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:32], [14:04]).

**Related** — [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]; [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]]; [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]].

confidence: supported

# Pass-Rush Pressure in Three Stages: Identify, Match, Score

**What it is** — S Min Hong (caption spelling "s Min Hong", "S Hong"; an applied scientist at AWS) presents work with the NFL Next Gen Stats team that replaces end-of-play pass-rush counts with a pressure measure through the whole play (1nt8hK2oYrE [00:00], [01:02]). Three problems are solved in sequence (1nt8hK2oYrE [02:38], [03:10], [03:42]):

1. **Blocker and rusher identification.** Label each player's role in the first seconds of the play.
2. **Rusher-blocker matchup.** Who blocks whom, including double teams ("Russia can be double teamed", caption for "rusher") and rushers left open.
3. **Pressure score.** An instantaneous 0 to 1 pressure probability across the play (see [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]).

Stages 1 and 2 automate what "human labelers" did by watching each clip, to save cost and manual labor (1nt8hK2oYrE [05:44], [06:15]). Inputs are static features (normalized initial positions at the snap, roles) and dynamic ones (position, velocity, acceleration, direction), standardized before training (1nt8hK2oYrE [06:46]). The data are the public Big Data Bowl tracking data (positions over time, velocity, acceleration, play outcomes) (1nt8hK2oYrE [04:12], [04:42], [05:14]).

Reported results: F1 of 0.99 for identification and "close 0.91" for matchup (caption spelling; 1nt8hK2oYrE [07:47]). Two model types were promising. The chosen one models the two tasks one after the other; the model name is garbled in captions ("Orum", "autog glom"), so the model type is unconfirmed (1nt8hK2oYrE [07:17], [07:47]). A graph neural network (players as nodes, relationships as edges) performed worse but was kept as a future direction because one model could do both tasks (1nt8hK2oYrE [08:17]). Ground truth for who blocks whom was hand labels from the NFL and PFF (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:08]), and the framework handles double and triple teams (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the staging: you cannot score pressure on a rusher until you know who is rushing and who is blocking him. Inference: splitting the problem lets stages 1 and 2 be validated against hand labels (F1) while stage 3 has no direct label.

**When to apply** — As a template for any play-level model that needs a role label before an outcome score: validate each stage separately against human labels where they exist and report the stage that has no label as such.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3; Explicit.) Inference: the build is justified only if defensive-line or protection staff have a question that end-of-play counts cannot answer. Baseline has no football pass-rush or position-tracking method to compare.

**When NOT to apply** — NFL tracking data and PFF hand labels; the baseline's technology stack (Catapult, Perch, Polar, VALD) lists no play-level tracking and labeling pipeline for football games. The F1 values are caption-rough and from one data set; the speaker gives no sample sizes. The model "didn't account for" team scheme or rushing and blocking strategy (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). Stage 3 has no accuracy figure (see [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a Jets versus Cowboys clip in which end-of-play stats credit only the players who recorded sacks, while other players closed on the quarterback without credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [00:32], [02:05]).

**Related** — [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]]; [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]; [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]]. A different tracking-data method on the same side of the ball: [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]] scores offensive linemen causally (SSAC25), while this pipeline is a descriptive, per-rusher pressure model. Library paper on the same problem: [[pipping-gamon-2026-opponent-adjusted-evaluation-of-nfl-pass-blocking-and-pass-rushing-performance]].

confidence: untested

# When the Output Is a Probability, Pick the Better-Calibrated Model

**What it is** — For the pressure score, Hong chose a random forest over "a complex neural network based or Transformer based model", because "model calibration" matters for a continuous score and the forest had better expected calibration error and maximum calibration error (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:26], [11:58], [12:28]). No calibration values are given.

He also notes an evaluation difficulty: a continuous pressure score is "kind of hard to evaluate", so he used a proxy, the maximum pressure a rusher or team puts on a passer, compared against PFF hurry, hit and sack labels, and reports "great accuracy" and better accuracy against hits and sacks, with a disparity across player groups and room to improve (the captions are garbled here; 1nt8hK2oYrE [10:54], [11:26], [11:58]).

**Why it works** — The speaker states calibration as the reason and gives no mechanism for why forests calibrate better than deep models here. Inference: a score read as a probability by a coach (for example, "70 percent chance this rusher gets home") is only honest if stated probabilities match observed frequencies.

**When to apply** — When model output will be shown as a probability or compared with a threshold (the talk uses a 75 percent "pressure zone" at 1nt8hK2oYrE [14:34]): compare candidate models on calibration error as well as accuracy, and prefer the simpler one when it calibrates better.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: a simple, inspectable model that Applied Performance staff can explain to coaches fits that rule better than a model nobody can interrogate.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no error values, no comparison table shown, only the speaker's statement. It applies to a probability output, and does not mean forests beat neural networks in general. The DeepQB talk (EeBgUCYhezc) used a feed-forward network and reported a calibration chart "fairly well calibrated" ([[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]]), so calibration is achievable with a neural network; the two talks do not compare.

**Example** — The speaker's choice itself: random forest over neural or Transformer models for the pressure score (1nt8hK2oYrE [12:28]).

**Related** — [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]; [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]; [[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]]; the CLIP talk also checks calibration and AUC for its propensity model, see [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]].
=================== principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play.md
confidence: untested

# Credit Pass-Rush Pressure Across the Whole Play, Not Only the Final Event

**What it is** — Hong's starting point: pass-rush statistics record only the outcome (the caption lists sacks and "how many Rush that he caused"; the terms hits and hurries are not named in that passage), so a rusher who closes on the quarterback but does not finish gets no credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [01:02], [01:34], [02:05]). The aim is to measure pressure "continuously applied throughout a play" and give credit to the defensive players who apply it (1nt8hK2oYrE [01:02], [02:38]). Outputs the speaker names: how long the passer is under pressure, and a "pressure zone", time with the score above 75 percent (1nt8hK2oYrE [14:34]).

In the example plays, three players generate high pressure, two early and one later who gets the sack (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00]), and in another the model credits two players with creating a lot of pressure where "a human label" credited one (the caption on the passer being forced "out of the sideline" is garbled, 1nt8hK2oYrE [13:32], [14:04]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no evidence the continuous credit is more accurate than the human label, only that it differs on the speaker's examples. Inference: counting outcomes only discards the time and path information that tracking data hold.

**When to apply** — When a coach's question is about a process that unfolds over a play and the available statistic records one endpoint. Ask whether tracking or film data can record the path, and who would act on it.

Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Explicit, Eric-authored SportSmith 2026-02-19, in method-baseline.md.) Inference: finer-grained credit is worth collecting only if it changes a decision about a player, and the talk reports no decision outcome.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: the evidence is two sample plays and no accuracy for the score itself (see [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]). It is NFL data, and the speaker names each team's blocking and rushing strategies as something the model did not account for (caption garbled: "specific pling and rushing uh strategies", 1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]); the speaker says the matchup stage can handle double and triple teams (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38]). The speaker's own Q&A answers confirm the score does not say whose pressure it is (1nt8hK2oYrE [21:40]), so using it to rank individual rushers goes beyond what the talk shows. A questioner argued the metric should weight how early pressure arrives (a hurry at 3 seconds beats one at 5.5), and the speaker agreed it was a good point (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38], [20:09]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a play where two rushers create high pressure early and a third late "who eventually get the sack" (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00]).

**Related** — [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]]; [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]. Contrast with [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]] (SSAC25), which argues about what a credited number can mean and applies to this kind of per-player credit.

# Pressure Score: A Blocker-Interference Feature and a Forgiving Label

**What it is** — Stage 3 of Hong's pipeline (see [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]]) models pressure as a probability that a rusher gets a hit, hurry or sack, on a 0 to 1 scale "at any point in time during the play" (1nt8hK2oYrE [08:47], [09:19]). Two design choices are the useful part.

**1. A blocker-interference feature.** For each rusher, an "area of interest" is set by distance and angle between the rusher and the passer, and the number of blockers inside it is counted, to measure the resistance the rusher may meet (1nt8hK2oYrE [09:51], [10:23]). It sits alongside the static and dynamic tracking features from the matchup stage and relative position, velocity and acceleration to the passer (1nt8hK2oYrE [09:51], [23:43]).

**2. A forgiving target.** Targets are the manually labeled PFF hurry, hit and sack, plus an engineered label based on the rusher's distance to the passer at a point in time (1nt8hK2oYrE [10:23], [10:54]). In Q&A he describes it as one rusher getting within one yard of the passer before one second; the captions are garbled, so the exact rule is uncertain (1nt8hK2oYrE [20:39]). The reason he gives: "it is not always the one player gets a sack", so a rusher who gets into the threshold area earns credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [22:12]).

Main drivers he gives (a light feature analysis, no values stated): the rusher's relative position to the passer, velocity and acceleration, initial position (who starts close), and how many blockers the rusher faces, with an open rusher more likely to generate pressure (1nt8hK2oYrE [17:37], [18:08], [18:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the intent (credit more than the sack-taker) but no test of the engineered label. Inference: a distance-based label turns a rare event (sack) into a more frequent one, which gives a model more signal to learn from.

**When to apply** — When an event label is rare and a process variable (distance, time) is available: consider a second, softer label, and disclose how it was set. Count obstructions between a mover and a target as a feature when tracking is available.

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-20). Inference: label consistency is the weakest point here; PFF hurry and hit labels are subjective hand labels, and the engineered label rule is not fully stated in the talk.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested. The speaker reports "great accuracy" against PFF labels and better calibration (expected and maximum calibration error) for the random forest, with no values (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:26] to [12:28]). No accuracy figure, no feature weights, no validation of the engineered label. The model "didn't actively account for" complex position features (1nt8hK2oYrE [18:38]), and team scheme and strategies are left as future work (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). It was trained on NFL data and PFF labels. The speaker did not check correlation with quarterback motion (1nt8hK2oYrE [23:13]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a passer forced toward the sideline after heavy pressure (caption wording: "forced... to be out of the... sideline", garbled), where the model credits two rushers (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:32], [14:04]).

**Related** — [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]; [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]]; [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]].

# Pass-Rush Pressure in Three Stages: Identify, Match, Score

**What it is** — S Min Hong (caption spelling "s Min Hong", "S Hong"; an applied scientist at AWS) presents work with the NFL Next Gen Stats team that replaces end-of-play pass-rush counts with a pressure measure through the whole play (1nt8hK2oYrE [00:00], [01:02]). Three problems are solved in sequence (1nt8hK2oYrE [02:38], [03:10], [03:42]):

1. **Blocker and rusher identification.** Label each player's role in the first seconds of the play.
2. **Rusher-blocker matchup.** Who blocks whom, including double teams ("Russia can be double teamed", caption for "rusher") and rushers left open.
3. **Pressure score.** An instantaneous 0 to 1 pressure probability across the play (see [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]).

Stages 1 and 2 automate what "human labelers" did by watching each clip, to save cost and manual labor (1nt8hK2oYrE [05:44], [06:15]). Inputs are static features (normalized initial positions at the snap, roles) and dynamic ones (position, velocity, acceleration, direction), standardized before training (1nt8hK2oYrE [06:46]). The data are the public Big Data Bowl tracking data (positions over time, velocity, acceleration, play outcomes) (1nt8hK2oYrE [04:12], [04:42], [05:14]).

Reported results: F1 of 0.99 for identification and "close 0.91" for matchup (caption spelling; 1nt8hK2oYrE [07:47]). Two model types were promising. The chosen one models the two tasks one after the other; the model name is garbled in captions ("Orum", "autog glom"), so the model type is unconfirmed (1nt8hK2oYrE [07:17], [07:47]). A graph neural network (players as nodes, relationships as edges) performed worse but was kept as a future direction because one model could do both tasks (1nt8hK2oYrE [08:17]). Ground truth for who blocks whom was hand labels from the NFL and PFF (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:08]), and the framework handles double and triple teams (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the staging: you cannot score pressure on a rusher until you know who is rushing and who is blocking him. Inference: splitting the problem lets stages 1 and 2 be validated against hand labels (F1) while stage 3 has no direct label.

**When to apply** — As a template for any play-level model that needs a role label before an outcome score: validate each stage separately against human labels where they exist and report the stage that has no label as such.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3; Explicit.) Inference: the build is justified only if defensive-line or protection staff have a question that end-of-play counts cannot answer. Baseline has no football pass-rush or position-tracking method to compare.

**When NOT to apply** — NFL tracking data and PFF hand labels; the baseline's technology stack (Catapult, Perch, Polar, VALD) lists no play-level tracking and labeling pipeline for football games. The F1 values are caption-rough and from one data set; the speaker gives no sample sizes. The model "didn't account for" team scheme or rushing and blocking strategy (1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]). Stage 3 has no accuracy figure (see [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a Jets versus Cowboys clip in which end-of-play stats credit only the players who recorded sacks, while other players closed on the quarterback without credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [00:32], [02:05]).

**Related** — [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]]; [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]; [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]]. A different tracking-data method on the same side of the ball: [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]] scores offensive linemen causally (SSAC25), while this pipeline is a descriptive, per-rusher pressure model. Library paper on the same problem: [[pipping-gamon-2026-opponent-adjusted-evaluation-of-nfl-pass-blocking-and-pass-rushing-performance]].

# When the Output Is a Probability, Pick the Better-Calibrated Model

**What it is** — For the pressure score, Hong chose a random forest over "a complex neural network based or Transformer based model", because "model calibration" matters for a continuous score and the forest had better expected calibration error and maximum calibration error (1nt8hK2oYrE [11:26], [11:58], [12:28]). No calibration values are given.

He also notes an evaluation difficulty: a continuous pressure score is "kind of hard to evaluate", so he used a proxy, the maximum pressure a rusher or team puts on a passer, compared against PFF hurry, hit and sack labels, and reports "great accuracy" and better accuracy against hits and sacks, with a disparity across player groups and room to improve (the captions are garbled here; 1nt8hK2oYrE [10:54], [11:26], [11:58]).

**Why it works** — The speaker states calibration as the reason and gives no mechanism for why forests calibrate better than deep models here. Inference: a score read as a probability by a coach (for example, "70 percent chance this rusher gets home") is only honest if stated probabilities match observed frequencies.

**When to apply** — When model output will be shown as a probability or compared with a threshold (the talk uses a 75 percent "pressure zone" at 1nt8hK2oYrE [14:34]): compare candidate models on calibration error as well as accuracy, and prefer the simpler one when it calibrates better.

Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) Inference: a simple, inspectable model that Applied Performance staff can explain to coaches fits that rule better than a model nobody can interrogate.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no error values, no comparison table shown, only the speaker's statement. It applies to a probability output, and does not mean forests beat neural networks in general. The DeepQB talk (EeBgUCYhezc) used a feed-forward network and reported a calibration chart "fairly well calibrated" ([[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]]), so calibration is achievable with a neural network; the two talks do not compare.

**Example** — The speaker's choice itself: random forest over neural or Transformer models for the pressure score (1nt8hK2oYrE [12:28]).

**Related** — [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]; [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]; [[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]]; the CLIP talk also checks calibration and AUC for its propensity model, see [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]].

# Credit Pass-Rush Pressure Across the Whole Play, Not Only the Final Event

**What it is** — Hong's starting point: pass-rush statistics record only the outcome (the caption lists sacks and "how many Rush that he caused"; the terms hits and hurries are not named in that passage), so a rusher who closes on the quarterback but does not finish gets no credit (1nt8hK2oYrE [01:02], [01:34], [02:05]). The aim is to measure pressure "continuously applied throughout a play" and give credit to the defensive players who apply it (1nt8hK2oYrE [01:02], [02:38]). Outputs the speaker names: how long the passer is under pressure, and a "pressure zone", time with the score above 75 percent (1nt8hK2oYrE [14:34]).

In the example plays, three players generate high pressure, two early and one later who gets the sack (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00]), and in another the model credits two players with creating a lot of pressure where "a human label" credited one (the caption on the passer being forced "out of the sideline" is garbled, 1nt8hK2oYrE [13:32], [14:04]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no evidence the continuous credit is more accurate than the human label, only that it differs on the speaker's examples. Inference: counting outcomes only discards the time and path information that tracking data hold.

**When to apply** — When a coach's question is about a process that unfolds over a play and the available statistic records one endpoint. Ask whether tracking or film data can record the path, and who would act on it.

Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Explicit, Eric-authored SportSmith 2026-02-19, in method-baseline.md.) Inference: finer-grained credit is worth collecting only if it changes a decision about a player, and the talk reports no decision outcome.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: the evidence is two sample plays and no accuracy for the score itself (see [[claim--pressure-score-evaluation-and-attribution-limits]]). It is NFL data, and the speaker names each team's blocking and rushing strategies as something the model did not account for (caption garbled: "specific pling and rushing uh strategies", 1nt8hK2oYrE [15:34]); the speaker says the matchup stage can handle double and triple teams (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38]). The speaker's own Q&A answers confirm the score does not say whose pressure it is (1nt8hK2oYrE [21:40]), so using it to rank individual rushers goes beyond what the talk shows. A questioner argued the metric should weight how early pressure arrives (a hurry at 3 seconds beats one at 5.5), and the speaker agreed it was a good point (1nt8hK2oYrE [19:38], [20:09]).

**Example** — The speaker's: a play where two rushers create high pressure early and a third late "who eventually get the sack" (1nt8hK2oYrE [13:00]).

**Related** — [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-three-stage-pipeline]]; [[framework--pass-rush-pressure-score-features-and-labels]]. Contrast with [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]] (SSAC25), which argues about what a credited number can mean and applies to this kind of per-player credit.

=================== claim--injury-risk-multiplier-robustness.md
confidence: untested

# Stress Test: With Injury Risk Two and Three Times Higher, the Search Model Gained Points and Injury Savings Shrank

**What it is** — To test robustness in higher-risk settings "not seen in our test data" (an intense run of cup matches, or contact sports such as rugby or American football), the presenters multiplied standard injury risks by two and three and again compared the search model with the greedy baseline (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:44], [12:15]). Reported: in higher-risk scenarios the search model outperformed the greedy model on season performance, with a 1.8% increase in expected points when risk was three times higher (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15]). As injury probability rose, the margin of injury reduction over the greedy baseline shrank, which they attribute to the strategy being forced into certain choices by multiple injuries, though injuries still fell "significantly" across all multipliers (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15], [12:46]). The talk gives no injury-reduction percentages for the 2x and 3x cases.

**Why it works** — The presenter's own explanation for the shrinking margin is forced decisions when many players are out; no further mechanism is given. Inference: when the available pool is thin, there is less room to rest anyone, so selection differences between the two rules narrow.

**When to apply** — As a reading aid for any rotation model: ask whether the benefit holds when risk is raised, and whether the injury margin shrinks as roster depth thins. Inference: for a football roster with positional depth limits, the shrinking-margin pattern is the more relevant half of this result.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a scaled version of a soccer injury model, not data from rugby or American football; the presenters list those sports as future work (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15], [14:18]). Multiplying risk by 2 or 3 assumes the same feature relationships hold at higher risk, which is not tested. No numbers beyond 1.8% are given, and it is a simulated result with no external validation. Do not cite it as evidence that the method works in contact sports.

**Example** — The speakers' own: injury risk at three times the standard level, search model 1.8% more expected points than greedy (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:15]).

**Related** — [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]; [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]].
=================== claim--modeled-wage-savings-from-fewer-injuries.md
confidence: untested

# Modeled Wage Savings: About 11% Less Salary Spent on Predicted Injuries

**What it is** — The presenters translate injuries into money using salary data from Capology: wages "spent" on players who are injured and so unavailable (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [12:46]). Reported: Brighton would have saved the most, a 22% reduction in salary cost tied to predicted injuries, and across all Premier League clubs the average was about 11% (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]). The motivating context was spoken twice with different figures: "almost $770 million" in injury costs in the top five European leagues, 30% more than the prior season, in the introduction (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01]), and "nearly $800 million" last season in the results (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:46]); the captions do not reconcile the two. Other context figures in the introduction: a 71% increase in injury severity after the winter World Cup and a 15% increase in the first three months of the Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01]). The conclusion repeats "approximately 13% fewer injuries" (base unclear: captions give "a 4.6% decrease in the squad and a 13% decrease in the ideal starting eleven" at [11:44]; see [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]) and "an 11% financial reduction in injury-related costs" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]).

**Why it works** — The figure is arithmetic on the model's own simulated injuries: fewer predicted injuries to high-wage players means fewer wages tied to unavailable players. The speakers give no further mechanism. Inference: the percentage depends on how the saved injuries are distributed across salary levels, which the talk does not show.

**When to apply** — As an example of expressing injury burden in the currency a club decision-maker uses. Inference: for a Baylor audience, the equivalent would be availability (games or practices missed by starters), not wages. Eric's baseline: coach-facing reports are built mostly by strength staff, with sport science staff providing reports where applicable (interview 2026-09-28, Q28, Explicit); no wage-based injury metric is in the baseline.

**When NOT to apply** — Not a measured saving: it comes from simulations with an imputed workload and no club data, and the $770 million and $800 million figures conflict inside the talk (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01], [12:46]). Professional soccer wages do not map to college athletics, where the cost is competitive and academic availability, not salary. Presented by Sentient Sports' CEO and co-founder (a startup interest); the lead author, Greg Everett, appears only by recorded video (K5a7C4b1Cwc [00:00], [00:30]).

**Example** — The speakers' own: Brighton, 22% lower salary cost tied to predicted injuries, versus an 11% average across clubs (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]).

**Related** — [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]; [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]].
=================== claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points.md
confidence: untested

# Simulated Result: Tree-Search Selection Cut Injuries at Similar Expected Points

**What it is** — The presenters compared their search-based selection with a greedy baseline that picks the team maximizing expected points for each match only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42], [10:12]). They ran thousands of simulations per season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:43], [11:14]). Reported: Brighton would have benefited most, with 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least, with 7.5% fewer in the ideal eleven; across all Premier League teams on average, 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal starting eleven, with similar expected points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14], [11:44]). The headline at the end, "approximately 13% on average" fewer injuries, matches the ideal-eleven figure, not the 4.6% squad figure, and the speaker does not say which (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]). Compared with real coaches, the search model's selections were about 76% similar and the greedy model's about 82%; the presenters suggest managers face short-term pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43]). They also say real technical directors often decide for short-term gains over long-term athlete protection (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:48]); he introduces it with "We also found," but no data or survey of directors is shown (Inference: it is a belief or anecdote, not a result of the simulation).

**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that the search values future availability and the greedy rule does not. They give no mechanism beyond the injury model's workload dependence; see [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]. Inference: because both models use the same injury model to score the outcome, the comparison measures how the injury model's own risk estimates change selections, not real injuries.

**When to apply** — As an illustration of what a rest-rotation decision model might claim, and of the size of benefit a vendor or paper could be expected to show. Inference: a claim of fewer injuries from a model should come with the injury model's validation, which this talk gives only partly (log loss 0.16, Pearson 0.77; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: all results are simulated from open data (StatsBomb 2017/18 and 2018/19 Premier League events, Transfermarkt injury history), with player load imputed and no club medical or training data (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [13:48], [17:53]). No club has used the recommendations, and the greedy comparison ran "for one season" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]; the caption does not name it, and the preceding model check used 2018/19), so it is a single simulated season. Substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). One league, professional soccer; do not apply the percentages to college football, where rotation is far more limited. One presenter introduces himself as the CEO and co-founder of a UK-based startup (K5a7C4b1Cwc [00:30]), so there is a commercial interest. The 13% versus 4.6% ambiguity above means the headline should be quoted with both figures.

**Example** — The speakers' own: Brighton, 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven at similar points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--injury-risk-multiplier-robustness]]; [[claim--modeled-wage-savings-from-fewer-injuries]]; [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]].
=================== claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history.md
confidence: untested

# In a Soccer Injury Model, Short- and Long-Term Workload and Detailed Injury History Mattered Most

**What it is** — The presenters report a gradient-boosted tree injury model (caption "XG boost") trained on injury-related features built from 2017-18 Premier League data and a historical career injury dataset (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). Inputs per player and match include workload from earlier selections, injury history (age, number of injuries) and context such as opponent and travel distance (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]). Using SHAP values, the least important group was contextual: travel to the game and rain. The next group, with somewhat more weight: days since the last injury, match-day temperature and age. The group that contributed most: the player's workload across matches, both short and long term, and the player's detailed injury history (K5a7C4b1Cwc [04:03], [04:33]). Testing: a 70/30 split with "five-block" cross-validation (caption spelling, probably five-fold), log loss 0.16, outperforming "many of the other base models we tested" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [09:42]); a Pearson correlation of 0.77 between the model's predictions and the 2018/19 Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). The talk does not say what was correlated (it reads as predicted versus observed injury outcomes) and gives no number of injuries or players.

**Why it works** — The speakers give no mechanism for why workload and injury history dominate; they report the SHAP ranking. Inference: prior injuries and recent load are the two inputs most directly tied to a specific player's tissue state, while travel and weather are shared across a squad.

**When to apply** — As a prior for what to log first when building an injury model with limited data: workload at more than one time scale, and a detailed injury history. Eric's baseline: there is no formal injury-risk model, and movement screens are collected and filed without changing programs (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit); this model's top inputs are workload and history, not screens.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the ranking is the model's own SHAP output, while the log loss and the 0.77 correlation validate predictions against a target the talk does not state ("with reality", K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). Player load was imputed from event data by a separate model, because tracking data is not open (K5a7C4b1Cwc [17:53]); there was no club medical data and no training load, so the workload feature misses training exposure, which a questioner pressed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:24], [18:54]). One league, two seasons, soccer, professional players. The presenter says it is a decision framework, "not an expert medical prediction model" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:54]). A correlation of 0.77 and a log loss of 0.16 are reported without class balance, so how the model would rank athletes in practice is unknown. Existing library caution: ACWR-style workload features carry the confounding concern in [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]], which this model's authors do not address.

**Example** — The speakers' own: for a player facing Watford, the model takes his workload from the previous selections, his injury history and age, and the opponent and travel distance, and outputs an injury probability for that match (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]] (workload-ratio confounding, contested). Existing library: [[research-papers/carey-2017-predictive-modelling-of-training-loads-and-injury-in-australian-football]].
=================== framework--adapt-maher-expected-points-model-with-player-skill.md
confidence: untested

# Make a Team-Level Match Model Sensitive to the Starting Eleven

**What it is** — The reward in the team-selection framework is expected points for a match. The presenters (Ryan Beiel and, in recorded video, the lead author Greg Everett, caption spellings) compute it from an adapted Maher model (caption "Maya"), a common soccer prediction model that assumes each team's scoring rate follows a Poisson distribution and learns offensive and defensive strengths from historical data to get win, draw and loss probabilities (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:05]). The original model works at team level and ignores individual selections, so they replaced the team-identity features with player-based numerical features: a player contribution model (caption "VAPE", likely a value-of-actions style model, not confirmed) supplies each player's skill value, and the combined skills of the chosen eleven feed a linear model (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:36], [06:06]). The output is converted to expected points per match, which also shows how important each match is to the season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [02:31], [06:06]). They report that over two Premier League seasons the adapted model achieved "similar performance, within the margins of error," to the original, with added flexibility to measure outcomes for individual selections (K5a7C4b1Cwc [06:06]).

**Why it works** — Replacing team identity with the skills of the named eleven lets the model respond to who plays (Inference: which is what a rest decision changes). The speakers give no numbers for the comparison (no error metric or margins shown in captions), so the equivalence to the original model is a statement, not a result you can cite. Inference: matching the original within error means the adaptation did not lose predictive power at team level; it does not show the player-level contributions are accurate.

**When to apply** — When a decision model needs a performance term that changes with the lineup. Inference: the check to copy is the one the speakers describe, comparing the adapted model against the original team-level model over the two seasons tested (the captions do not say the data were held out) before using it as a reward.

**When NOT to apply** — Two Premier League seasons, StatsBomb event data for 2017/18 and 2018/19 (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11]). Soccer scoring is Poisson-like, which is the model's central assumption; do not carry the form to American football scoring without checking. The player skill model's name and construction are garbled in the captions, so the skill values cannot be reproduced from this talk. Untested in this library: no comparison numbers are available.

**Example** — The speakers' own: slide jerseys carrying numerical skill values for each player of a team, summed into the starting eleven's strength for a match (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:36], [06:06]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]].
=================== framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts.md
confidence: untested

# Frame Lineup Selection as a Sequential Decision: Markov Decision Process Solved by Monte Carlo Tree Search

**What it is** — The presenter (Ryan Beiel, caption spelling, CEO of the startup Sentient Sports) and the lead author (Greg Everett, caption spelling, in recorded video segments) describe a framework for choosing a soccer starting eleven that balances winning now against injury risk later (K5a7C4b1Cwc [00:00], [01:31], [02:01]). Each week: a team plans its upcoming matches; every player has a skill rating and a next-match injury probability, both from separate models; an optimization picks the 11 starters; the state updates for injuries that occurred and for player use; repeat week after week (K5a7C4b1Cwc [02:01], [02:31]). The coach's problem is framed as a Markov decision process (MDP) whose objective is to maximize expected points over the season while balancing the chance of winning upcoming matches against injury risk to key players (K5a7C4b1Cwc [06:37]). Because the decision space is large, they approximate the optimum with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS). Nodes are MDP states (current match, player injury risks, existing injuries), branches are team selections, and leaf nodes are the next match with updated injuries (K5a7C4b1Cwc [07:07]). The loop: selection by an upper confidence bound heuristic, expansion by "progressive broadening," simulation of the rest of the season assuming the coach picks the most qualified team, and back-propagation of expected points to the root (K5a7C4b1Cwc [07:38], [08:09], [08:39]). It repeats thousands or millions of times and returns the selection with the highest expected value (K5a7C4b1Cwc [08:39]).

**Why it works** — The speakers' argument is that a greedy choice each week ignores the later cost of an injury, while the tree search values future matches (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12]). Their stated expectation is that resting a player lowers workload and so injury risk, if the rest is timed so that performance is not sacrificed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). The speakers give no evidence in the talk that rest at a given moment lowers a specific player's risk beyond what their injury model assumes. Inference: the framework is only as good as the injury-probability model feeding it; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]].

**When to apply** — As a design pattern for any roster-rotation question where today's choice changes tomorrow's availability (rest rotation, minutes management). Inference: the pieces that transfer are the separation of three parts (a per-player availability or injury model, a per-lineup performance model, and a search over sequences) and the explicit horizon; see [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]]. Eric's baseline: football has an in-season game-week structure (Sunday off, Monday heavy lift, hard practice ending 72 hours before a Saturday game, interview 2026-09-28, Q15, Explicit) and a bye-week rule: "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps" (Q17, Explicit); rest decisions are made by schedule design and coach judgment, not by a search model.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested outside simulation. The presenter says it is built on freely available open data, is "a framework for decision-making rather than ... an expert medical prediction model," and that a volunteer team would have to be found and a coach convinced to follow it (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48], [18:54]). Resting is all or nothing for a full match; substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). It was tested on Premier League data only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18], [19:54]). American football and rugby are named only as future work or as higher-injury-risk scenarios (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:44], [14:18]). Inference: American football differs in roster size, position-specific roles, contact injuries and limited free rotation. The speaker has a startup interest in the method.

**Example** — The speakers' own: for N'Golo Kante, the model kept his predicted injury probability low through the season except the final stretch, where the real Chelsea rested him and the model chose to start him (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]). A single example, shown as an illustration.

**Related** — [[framework--adapt-maher-expected-points-model-with-player-skill]]; [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]; [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/martnez-ruiz-undated-a-decision-driven-framework-for-interdisciplinary-player-evaluation-in-elite-football]] (a decision-driven framework for football player evaluation).
=================== heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match.md
confidence: untested

# Plan Rest Over a Rolling Horizon, Not Just the Next Match

**What it is** — Two points from the talk. First, the greedy rule of picking the best team for each match ignores long-term injury and absence risk, and the presenters found real coaches' selections closer to the greedy model (82% similar) than to their search model (76%), which they attribute to short-term job pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43], [14:48]). Second, in the Q&A, a questioner (not named) compared it to an American "survivor pool" in which picking the best matchups early corners you later, and suggested optimizing only the next X games and re-optimizing as injuries occur and player skill estimates change (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49], [16:20]). The presenter replied that the model has a parameter for how many games forward to simulate, from the end of the season to a five-game window moved forward week by week (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:51]).

**Why it works** — The questioner's reason is that a short window lets the coach re-plan with real information on who is available (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:20]); the presenter agrees the horizon can be set as a parameter (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:51]). The presenter gives no result comparing a five-game window with a full-season horizon. Inference: a shorter horizon trades some foresight for robustness to model error, since injury and skill estimates drift.

**When to apply** — When planning rest or playing time across a congested stretch: set an explicit horizon (for example, the next several games), re-plan each week with updated availability, and name what the greedy option would be so the cost of the short-term choice is visible. Eric's baseline: in football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason the priority window (interview 2026-09-28, Q14, Explicit), and bye weeks give players with few snaps harder practice (Q17, Explicit). Inference: those are horizon decisions already made by calendar, and the heuristic asks whether any are made match by match instead.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the horizon parameter is described, not evaluated, and the greedy-versus-search similarity numbers come from StatsBomb event data for two Premier League seasons, 2017/18 and 2018/19 (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [10:12]); the presenters call their data freely available and open source (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). The explanation of coaches' choices (job pressure) is the presenters' belief. In football the roster and the game schedule give one game a week and no free rotation, so the "next X games" horizon is short already.

**Example** — The questioner's own analogy: a survivor-pool player who uses all the best teams early has nothing left late in the season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]].

**What it is** — The presenters translate injuries into money using salary data from Capology: wages "spent" on players who are injured and so unavailable (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [12:46]).
