# Simulated Result: Tree-Search Selection Cut Injuries at Similar Expected Points

**What it is** — The presenters compared their search-based selection with a greedy baseline that picks the team maximizing expected points for each match only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42], [10:12]). They ran thousands of simulations per season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:43], [11:14]). Reported: Brighton would have benefited most, with 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven; Chelsea least, with 7.5% fewer in the ideal eleven; across all Premier League teams on average, 4.6% fewer squad injuries and 13% fewer in the ideal starting eleven, with similar expected points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14], [11:44]). The headline at the end, "approximately 13% on average" fewer injuries, matches the ideal-eleven figure, not the 4.6% squad figure, and the speaker does not say which (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]). Compared with real coaches, the search model's selections were about 76% similar and the greedy model's about 82%; the presenters suggest managers face short-term pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43]). They also say real technical directors often decide for short-term gains over long-term athlete protection (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:48]); he introduces it with "We also found," but no data or survey of directors is shown (Inference: it is a belief or anecdote, not a result of the simulation).

**Why it works** — The speakers' explanation is that the search values future availability and the greedy rule does not. They give no mechanism beyond the injury model's workload dependence; see [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]. Inference: because both models use the same injury model to score the outcome, the comparison measures how the injury model's own risk estimates change selections, not real injuries.

**When to apply** — As an illustration of what a rest-rotation decision model might claim, and of the size of benefit a vendor or paper could be expected to show. Inference: a claim of fewer injuries from a model should come with the injury model's validation, which this talk gives only partly (log loss 0.16, Pearson 0.77; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: all results are simulated from open data (StatsBomb 2017/18 and 2018/19 Premier League events, Transfermarkt injury history), with player load imputed and no club medical or training data (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [13:48], [17:53]). No club has used the recommendations, and the greedy comparison ran "for one season" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]; the caption does not name it, and the preceding model check used 2018/19), so it is a single simulated season. Substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). One league, professional soccer; do not apply the percentages to college football, where rotation is far more limited. One presenter introduces himself as the CEO and co-founder of a UK-based startup (K5a7C4b1Cwc [00:30]), so there is a commercial interest. The 13% versus 4.6% ambiguity above means the headline should be quoted with both figures.

**Example** — The speakers' own: Brighton, 15.5% fewer squad injuries and 23% fewer in the ideal eleven at similar points (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:14]).

# In a Soccer Injury Model, Short- and Long-Term Workload and Detailed Injury History Mattered Most

**What it is** — The presenters report a gradient-boosted tree injury model (caption "XG boost") trained on injury-related features built from 2017-18 Premier League data and a historical career injury dataset (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). Inputs per player and match include workload from earlier selections, injury history (age, number of injuries) and context such as opponent and travel distance (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]). Using SHAP values, the least important group was contextual: travel to the game and rain. The next group, with somewhat more weight: days since the last injury, match-day temperature and age. The group that contributed most: the player's workload across matches, both short and long term, and the player's detailed injury history (K5a7C4b1Cwc [04:03], [04:33]). Testing: a 70/30 split with "five-block" cross-validation (caption spelling, probably five-fold), log loss 0.16, outperforming "many of the other base models we tested" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [09:42]); a Pearson correlation of 0.77 between the model's predictions and the 2018/19 Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). The talk does not say what was correlated (it reads as predicted versus observed injury outcomes) and gives no number of injuries or players.

**Why it works** — The speakers give no mechanism for why workload and injury history dominate; they report the SHAP ranking. Inference: prior injuries and recent load are the two inputs most directly tied to a specific player's tissue state, while travel and weather are shared across a squad.

**When to apply** — As a prior for what to log first when building an injury model with limited data: workload at more than one time scale, and a detailed injury history. Eric's baseline: there is no formal injury-risk model, and movement screens are collected and filed without changing programs (interview 2026-09-28, Q12, Explicit); this model's top inputs are workload and history, not screens.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the ranking is the model's own SHAP output, while the log loss and the 0.77 correlation validate predictions against a target the talk does not state ("with reality", K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:42]). Player load was imputed from event data by a separate model, because tracking data is not open (K5a7C4b1Cwc [17:53]); there was no club medical data and no training load, so the workload feature misses training exposure, which a questioner pressed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:24], [18:54]). One league, two seasons, soccer, professional players. The presenter says it is a decision framework, "not an expert medical prediction model" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [18:54]). A correlation of 0.77 and a log loss of 0.16 are reported without class balance, so how the model would rank athletes in practice is unknown. Existing library caution: ACWR-style workload features carry the confounding concern in [[principle--training-schedule-confounds-acwr-and-injury]], which this model's authors do not address.

**Example** — The speakers' own: for a player facing Watford, the model takes his workload from the previous selections, his injury history and age, and the opponent and travel distance, and outputs an injury probability for that match (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:32], [04:03]).

# Make a Team-Level Match Model Sensitive to the Starting Eleven

**What it is** — The reward in the team-selection framework is expected points for a match. The presenters (Ryan Beiel and, in recorded video, the lead author Greg Everett, caption spellings) compute it from an adapted Maher model (caption "Maya"), a common soccer prediction model that assumes each team's scoring rate follows a Poisson distribution and learns offensive and defensive strengths from historical data to get win, draw and loss probabilities (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:05]). The original model works at team level and ignores individual selections, so they replaced the team-identity features with player-based numerical features: a player contribution model (caption "VAPE", likely a value-of-actions style model, not confirmed) supplies each player's skill value, and the combined skills of the chosen eleven feed a linear model (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:36], [06:06]). The output is converted to expected points per match, which also shows how important each match is to the season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [02:31], [06:06]). They report that over two Premier League seasons the adapted model achieved "similar performance, within the margins of error," to the original, with added flexibility to measure outcomes for individual selections (K5a7C4b1Cwc [06:06]).

**Why it works** — Replacing team identity with the skills of the named eleven lets the model respond to who plays (Inference: which is what a rest decision changes). The speakers give no numbers for the comparison (no error metric or margins shown in captions), so the equivalence to the original model is a statement, not a result you can cite. Inference: matching the original within error means the adaptation did not lose predictive power at team level; it does not show the player-level contributions are accurate.

**When to apply** — When a decision model needs a performance term that changes with the lineup. Inference: the check to copy is the one the speakers describe, comparing the adapted model against the original team-level model over the two seasons tested (the captions do not say the data were held out) before using it as a reward.

**When NOT to apply** — Two Premier League seasons, StatsBomb event data for 2017/18 and 2018/19 (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11]). Soccer scoring is Poisson-like, which is the model's central assumption; do not carry the form to American football scoring without checking. The player skill model's name and construction are garbled in the captions, so the skill values cannot be reproduced from this talk. Untested in this library: no comparison numbers are available.

**Example** — The speakers' own: slide jerseys carrying numerical skill values for each player of a team, summed into the starting eleven's strength for a match (K5a7C4b1Cwc [05:36], [06:06]).

# Frame Lineup Selection as a Sequential Decision: Markov Decision Process Solved by Monte Carlo Tree Search

**What it is** — The presenter (Ryan Beiel, caption spelling, CEO of the startup Sentient Sports) and the lead author (Greg Everett, caption spelling, in recorded video segments) describe a framework for choosing a soccer starting eleven that balances winning now against injury risk later (K5a7C4b1Cwc [00:00], [01:31], [02:01]). Each week: a team plans its upcoming matches; every player has a skill rating and a next-match injury probability, both from separate models; an optimization picks the 11 starters; the state updates for injuries that occurred and for player use; repeat week after week (K5a7C4b1Cwc [02:01], [02:31]). The coach's problem is framed as a Markov decision process (MDP) whose objective is to maximize expected points over the season while balancing the chance of winning upcoming matches against injury risk to key players (K5a7C4b1Cwc [06:37]). Because the decision space is large, they approximate the optimum with Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS). Nodes are MDP states (current match, player injury risks, existing injuries), branches are team selections, and leaf nodes are the next match with updated injuries (K5a7C4b1Cwc [07:07]). The loop: selection by an upper confidence bound heuristic, expansion by "progressive broadening," simulation of the rest of the season assuming the coach picks the most qualified team, and back-propagation of expected points to the root (K5a7C4b1Cwc [07:38], [08:09], [08:39]). It repeats thousands or millions of times and returns the selection with the highest expected value (K5a7C4b1Cwc [08:39]).

**Why it works** — The speakers' argument is that a greedy choice each week ignores the later cost of an injury, while the tree search values future matches (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12]). Their stated expectation is that resting a player lowers workload and so injury risk, if the rest is timed so that performance is not sacrificed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). The speakers give no evidence in the talk that rest at a given moment lowers a specific player's risk beyond what their injury model assumes. Inference: the framework is only as good as the injury-probability model feeding it; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]].

**When to apply** — As a design pattern for any roster-rotation question where today's choice changes tomorrow's availability (rest rotation, minutes management). Inference: the pieces that transfer are the separation of three parts (a per-player availability or injury model, a per-lineup performance model, and a search over sequences) and the explicit horizon; see [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]]. Eric's baseline: football has an in-season game-week structure (Sunday off, Monday heavy lift, hard practice ending 72 hours before a Saturday game, interview 2026-09-28, Q15, Explicit) and a bye-week rule: "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps" (Q17, Explicit); rest decisions are made by schedule design and coach judgment, not by a search model.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested outside simulation. The presenter says it is built on freely available open data, is "a framework for decision-making rather than ... an expert medical prediction model," and that a volunteer team would have to be found and a coach convinced to follow it (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48], [18:54]). Resting is all or nothing for a full match; substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). It was tested on Premier League data only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18], [19:54]). American football and rugby are named only as future work or as higher-injury-risk scenarios (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:44], [14:18]). Inference: American football differs in roster size, position-specific roles, contact injuries and limited free rotation. The speaker has a startup interest in the method.

**Example** — The speakers' own: for N'Golo Kante, the model kept his predicted injury probability low through the season except the final stretch, where the real Chelsea rested him and the model chose to start him (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]). A single example, shown as an illustration.

**Related** — [[framework--adapt-maher-expected-points-model-with-player-skill]]; [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]; [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]]. Existing library: [[research-papers/martnez-ruiz-undated-a-decision-driven-framework-for-interdisciplinary-player-evaluation-in-elite-football]] (a decision-driven framework for football player evaluation).

# Plan Rest Over a Rolling Horizon, Not Just the Next Match

**What it is** — Two points from the talk. First, the greedy rule of picking the best team for each match ignores long-term injury and absence risk, and the presenters found real coaches' selections closer to the greedy model (82% similar) than to their search model (76%), which they attribute to short-term job pressure (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12], [10:43], [14:48]). Second, in the Q&A, a questioner (not named) compared it to an American "survivor pool" in which picking the best matchups early corners you later, and suggested optimizing only the next X games and re-optimizing as injuries occur and player skill estimates change (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49], [16:20]). The presenter replied that the model has a parameter for how many games forward to simulate, from the end of the season to a five-game window moved forward week by week (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:51]).

**Why it works** — The questioner's reason is that a short window lets the coach re-plan with real information on who is available (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:20]); the presenter agrees the horizon can be set as a parameter (K5a7C4b1Cwc [16:51]). The presenter gives no result comparing a five-game window with a full-season horizon. Inference: a shorter horizon trades some foresight for robustness to model error, since injury and skill estimates drift.

**When to apply** — When planning rest or playing time across a congested stretch: set an explicit horizon (for example, the next several games), re-plan each week with updated availability, and name what the greedy option would be so the cost of the short-term choice is visible. Eric's baseline: in football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason the priority window (interview 2026-09-28, Q14, Explicit), and bye weeks give players with few snaps harder practice (Q17, Explicit). Inference: those are horizon decisions already made by calendar, and the heuristic asks whether any are made match by match instead.

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the horizon parameter is described, not evaluated, and the greedy-versus-search similarity numbers come from StatsBomb event data for two Premier League seasons, 2017/18 and 2018/19 (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [10:12]); the presenters call their data freely available and open source (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). The explanation of coaches' choices (job pressure) is the presenters' belief. In football the roster and the game schedule give one game a week and no free rotation, so the "next X games" horizon is short already.

**Example** — The questioner's own analogy: a survivor-pool player who uses all the best teams early has nothing left late in the season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [15:49]).

**Related** — [[framework--injury-aware-team-selection-as-mdp-with-mcts]]; [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]].

lines: # Modeled Wage Savings: About 11% Less Salary Spent on Predicted Injuries

-**What it is** — The presenters translate injuries into money using salary data from Capology: wages "spent" on players who are injured and so unavailable (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [12:46]). Reported: Brighton would have saved the most, a 22% reduction in salary cost tied to predicted injuries, and across all Premier League clubs the average was about 11% (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]). The motivating context was spoken twice with different figures: "almost $770 million" in injury costs in the top five European leagues, 30% more than the prior season, in the introduction (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01]), and "nearly $800 million" last season in the results (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:46]); the captions do not reconcile the two. Other context figures in the introduction: a 71% increase in injury severity after the winter World Cup and a 15% increase in the first three months of the Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01]). The conclusion repeats "approximately 13% fewer injuries" (base unclear: captions give "a 4.6% decrease in the squad and a 13% decrease in the ideal starting eleven" at [11:44]; see [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]) and "an 11% financial reduction in injury-related costs" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]).

+**What it is** — The presenters translate injuries into money using salary data from Capology, as "salary cost reduction due to predicted injuries" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [09:11], [12:46]); how the cost is computed is not described. Reported: Brighton would have saved the most, a 22% reduction in salary cost tied to predicted injuries, and across all Premier League clubs the average was about 11% (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:16]). The motivating context was spoken twice with different figures: "almost $770 million" in injury costs in the top five European leagues, 30% more than the prior season, in the introduction (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01]), and "nearly $800 million" last season in the results (K5a7C4b1Cwc [12:46]); the captions do not reconcile the two. Other context figures in the introduction: a 71% increase in injury severity after the winter World Cup and a 15% increase in the first three months of the Premier League season (K5a7C4b1Cwc [01:01]). The conclusion repeats "approximately 13% fewer injuries" (base unclear: captions give "a 4.6% decrease in the squad and a 13% decrease in the ideal starting eleven" at [11:44]; see [[claim--search-selection-cuts-simulated-injuries-at-similar-points]]) and "an 11% financial reduction in injury-related costs" (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18]).

**Why it works** — The figure is arithmetic on the model's own simulated injuries: fewer predicted injuries to high-wage players means fewer wages tied to unavailable players. The speakers give no further mechanism. Inference: the percentage depends on how the saved injuries are distributed across salary levels, which the talk does not show.

**Why it works** — The speakers' argument is that a greedy choice each week ignores the later cost of an injury, while the tree search values future matches (K5a7C4b1Cwc [10:12]). Their stated expectation is that resting a player lowers workload and so injury risk, if the rest is timed so that performance is not sacrificed (K5a7C4b1Cwc [03:02]). The speakers give no evidence in the talk that rest at a given moment lowers a specific player's risk beyond what their injury model assumes. Inference: the framework is only as good as the injury-probability model feeding it; see [[claim--soccer-injury-model-top-features-are-workload-and-injury-history]].

-**When to apply** — As a design pattern for any roster-rotation question where today's choice changes tomorrow's availability (rest rotation, minutes management). Inference: the pieces that transfer are the separation of three parts (a per-player availability or injury model, a per-lineup performance model, and a search over sequences) and the explicit horizon; see [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]]. Eric's baseline: football has an in-season game-week structure (Sunday off, Monday heavy lift, hard practice ending 72 hours before a Saturday game, interview 2026-09-28, Q15, Explicit) and a bye-week rule: "guys that aren't getting a ton of play will probably practice harder that week than guys that have gotten a ton of snaps" (Q17, Explicit); rest decisions are made by schedule design and coach judgment, not by a search model.

Inference: the pieces that transfer are the separation of three parts (a per-player availability or injury model, a per-lineup performance model, and a search over sequences) and the explicit horizon; see [[heuristic--plan-rest-over-a-horizon-not-the-next-match]]. Inference: rest at Baylor is therefore set by schedule design and coach judgment, not by a search model.

-**When NOT to apply** — Untested outside simulation. The presenter says it is built on freely available open data, is "a framework for decision-making rather than ... an expert medical prediction model," and that a volunteer team would have to be found and a coach convinced to follow it (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48], [18:54]). Resting is all or nothing for a full match; substitutions are not modeled (K5a7C4b1Cwc [13:48]). It was tested on Premier League data only (K5a7C4b1Cwc [14:18], [19:54]). American football and rugby are named only as future work or as higher-injury-risk scenarios (K5a7C4b1Cwc [11:44], [14:18]). Inference: American football differs in roster size, position-specific roles, contact injuries and limited free rotation. The speaker has a startup interest in the method.

# Case study: Chris Paul and the Phoenix trio, and two other anecdotes

**What it is** — The speakers open with the 2020-21 Phoenix Suns. After acquiring Chris Paul, the team (as captioned) started "11 and N" and went "about 40 and 20 something" the rest of the way; the exact records are garbled in the captions (o4rMbhsdk0I [02:00]). Early on, points per attempt on Paul's passes to teammates was "well below league average" (caption: "8 low well below"), then improved and, in the second half of the season, the team was "one of the most dominant" (o4rMbhsdk0I [02:31]). Later the speakers return to three Phoenix shooters, listed by the speaker alongside Paul (captions: "Devon Booker, Mel Bridges, DeAndre Aton"): their results moved "from 81 points per 100 shots to 93", about half from shot selection and half from accuracy, and more up to about 200 shots (o4rMbhsdk0I [16:57], [17:27]). They label these rule-of-thumb numbers (o4rMbhsdk0I [17:27]). The video description quotes different figures (eFG% 46.6% on 74 shots, then 72.3% over the last 20 games); those do not appear in the captions and were not checked here.

Two more anecdotes motivated the study: Kyrie Irving at 1.15 points per attempt with Brooklyn, weaker after moving to Dallas, better the next year with Luca (o4rMbhsdk0I [03:31]); and Russell Westbrook at 1.03 on shots from LeBron in his second year, down again at the Clippers, up the next year (o4rMbhsdk0I [04:02], [04:34]). The speakers call these anecdotes and say they wanted to study them systematically (o4rMbhsdk0I [04:34]). A line attributed to a former boss is quoted: a midseason acquisition "makes you worse before it makes you better" (o4rMbhsdk0I [03:01]).

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for these cases specifically; they are offered as motivation. The accuracy explanations the speaker offers (confidence, rhythm, pass placement) are in [[claim--familiarity-gain-splits-between-shot-selection-and-accuracy]].

**When to apply** — As an illustration of the pattern to look for when a new pairing joins, not as evidence for it. Inference: when grading a new pairing, flag whether the sample sits in the steep early stretch.

**When NOT to apply** — These are single cases chosen because they fit the story, with no control for injury, roster, schedule or coaching change, and the Phoenix trio figure is a rule of thumb from a slide. The 81-to-93 figures are per 100 shots for one trio. Do not cite them as an effect size. The better evidence is the broader pass-and-shoot analysis (the 1600 passer-shooter pairs the speaker cites are a count "for context" for pairs with 10 to 50 catch-and-shoot attempts in 2023-24, not the full dataset) (see [[claim--teammate-familiarity-improves-catch-and-shoot-shot-quality]]).

**Example** — The case is itself the example: Paul's passes to the three Phoenix shooters, 81 to 93 points per 100 shots (o4rMbhsdk0I [17:27]).

**Related** — [[claim--teammate-familiarity-improves-catch-and-shoot-shot-quality]], [[claim--familiarity-gain-splits-between-shot-selection-and-accuracy]].

# About half of the familiarity gain is shot selection and half is accuracy

**What it is** — The speakers report that the accuracy curve (actual minus expected points) has nearly the same shape as the shot-selection curve, with about 7% improvement after 50 shots and gradual gain afterward, and a partial reset next season (o4rMbhsdk0I [12:18], [12:49]). Over the first 50 shots, they say each accounts for roughly half of the overall improvement: "about 50% of the gain is just that shot quality and then the other 50% is the accuracy" (o4rMbhsdk0I [15:54]). The 7% line at [16:26] is garbled in the captions ("a 7% field goal percentage"), so the unit of the accuracy gain is not clear.

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism that the model tests. The speaker, a former coach, offers explanations that are not in the model: confidence ("your brain doesn't get in the way"), rhythm and timing, and passer-specific preferences for pass placement (chest-high, a lower shooting pocket, left or right) (o4rMbhsdk0I [13:52], [14:22], [15:23]). The speaker says "we don't know because it's not in the model" (o4rMbhsdk0I [13:52]). In the Q&A the speakers say the accuracy piece cannot be separated into better off-ball screening versus better passing with current data (o4rMbhsdk0I [40:33], [41:03]). Inference: confidence and rhythm are hypotheses until measured.

**When to apply** — As a reminder to split any "got better together" result into what was chosen and what was executed before acting on it. Inference: a unit that improves because it picks better opportunities needs a different response (play design, spacing) from one that executes better (reps, timing).

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested because the 50/50 split rests on one model and a slide, with no uncertainty shown, and the accuracy side depends on an assumed 1.2 expected-points baseline (o4rMbhsdk0I [12:18]). The speakers call their numbers rule of thumb (o4rMbhsdk0I [17:27]). Do not read the split as exact or as portable to other sports or play types. The coaching explanations are one speaker's view, not findings.

**Example** — The talk's own illustration is the Phoenix trio (see [[case-study--phoenix-suns-chris-paul-familiarity-ramp]]).

**Related** — [[claim--teammate-familiarity-improves-catch-and-shoot-shot-quality]], [[framework--familiarity-counter-log-log-shot-quality-model]].
=================== claim--familiarity-gains-diminish-across-seasons.md
confidence: untested

# Familiarity carries over between seasons with diminishing marginal gains

**What it is** — Asked about diminishing returns, a speaker answers that a third season would start lower than the peak at the end of season two but "not that different from the start of the second season", so marginal gains keep declining season to season (o4rMbhsdk0I [19:31]). The data set does not hold enough pairs who played together for long to find a theoretical maximum, but "two, three seasons together is beneficial" (o4rMbhsdk0I [20:01]). "description": "When Chris Paul signed with the Phoenix Suns ahead of the 2020-21 season, he had never played with their three most frequent shooters (Devin Booker, DeAndre Ayton, and Mikal Bridges). He didn't know how they moved on the court, or where they wanted to receive a pass to most complement their shooting motion. The lack of familiarity with his teammates showed, as during the first two months of the season, the trio had an eFG% of 46.6% on the 74 shots off of Paul passes. Throughout the season, the familiarity between teammates grew with reps both in games and in practice. Paul learned how to setup his teammates to maximize their production. The increased familiarity between the teammates showed

-**What it is** — The speakers open with the 2020-21 Phoenix Suns. After acquiring Chris Paul, the team (as captioned) started "11 and N" and went "about 40 and 20 something" the rest of the way; the exact records are garbled in the captions (o4rMbhsdk0I [02:00]). Early on, points per attempt on Paul's passes to teammates was "well below league average" (caption: "8 low well below"), then improved and, in the second half of the season, the team was "one of the most dominant" (o4rMbhsdk0I [02:31]). Later the speakers return to three Phoenix shooters, listed by the speaker alongside Paul (captions: "Devon Booker, Mel Bridges, DeAndre Aton"): their results moved "from 81 points per 100 shots to 93", about half from shot selection and half from accuracy, and more up to about 200 shots (o4rMbhsdk0I [16:57], [17:27]). They label these rule-of-thumb numbers (o4rMbhsdk0I [17:27]). The video description quotes different figures (eFG% 46.6% on 74 shots, then 72.3% over the last 20 games); those do not appear in the captions and were not checked here.

+**What it is** — The speakers open with the Phoenix Suns "a couple years ago," after the bubble (the 2020-21 season is named only in the video description) (o4rMbhsdk0I [01:30], [02:00]). After acquiring Chris Paul, the team (as captioned) started "11 and N" and went "about 40 and 20 something" the rest of the way; the exact records are garbled in the captions (o4rMbhsdk0I [02:00]). They label these rule-of-thumb numbers (o4rMbhsdk0I [17:27]). The video description quotes different figures (eFG% 46.6% on 74 shots, then 72.3% over the last 20 games); those do not appear in the captions and were not checked here.

Two more anecdotes motivated the study: Kyrie Irving at 1.15 points per attempt with Brooklyn, weaker after moving to Dallas, better the next year with Luca (o4rMbhsdk0I [03:31]); and Russell Westbrook at 1.03 on shots from LeBron in his second year, down again at the Clippers, up the next year (o4rMbhsdk0I [04:02], [04:34]). The speakers call these anecdotes and say they wanted to study them systematically (o4rMbhsdk0I [04:34]). A line attributed to a former boss is quoted: a midseason acquisition "makes you worse before it makes you better" (o4rMbhsdk0I [03:01]).

**When to apply** — When asking whether a group of pairs improves with repetition: first fix a baseline that prices the opportunity, then count shared repetitions. Inference: in football this needs a play-level expected-value or grade baseline for the chosen play type and a reliable tally of shared reps for each pair. Eric's baseline: "Testing protocol has to be exactly repeatable over time ... or the resulting data cannot be trusted for comparison." (Inferred (transcript).) Inference: the same holds for how attempts are counted here.

# Two CLIP Plays: A Failed Block and Clean Protection

**What it is** — Jenkins shows two plays, each with a field map shaded by each lineman's value, a time series every tenth of a second, and a whole-line value (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [04:31], [05:01]).

**Failed block.** A Tua Tagovailoa completion to a receiver (captions: "Tua tangaloa", "mik aeki") where two linemen "fail their assignment" and the quarterback is pressured. Green means above expectation and red below; the model flags the two linemen in red as lowering the chance of a successful play (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:31], [04:01], [04:31]). Values change over time with each lineman's features. The whole-line value starts at 0.10 to 0.15 (captions "01 to 0.15"), read as 10 to 15 percent of the completion attributable to the line, something he says correlation-only metrics "cannot state" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [05:01]).

**Clean protection.** A Jimmy Garoppolo completion to Deebo Samuel (captions "Jimmy Garoppolo", "Debo Samuel") with plenty of space; shading runs purple to green because everyone contributed positively and no pressure was allowed. Best performers named: "Daniel brunskill" (caption spelling); one of the worst, Trent Williams, "but he's still positive". The line total is 0.6 to 0.8 (captions "6 to8"), read as 60 to 80 percent of the play attributable to the line (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [05:31], [06:01]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for why the line share differs so much between plays (10 to 15 percent versus 60 to 80 percent), and the talk does not explain it. Inference: because the estimand is the effect of allowing pressure, a play with no pressure allowed makes the positive values hard to interpret as that effect, and the speaker does not say how.

**When to apply** — As a worked pair to test understanding of the output: one can read a lineman's value as a play-level, time-varying credit. Inference: a usable film-review exercise is to check the two flagged linemen against film for the assignment failure the speaker describes.

Eric's baseline: Eric's baseline has no football-play method; the closest standing rule is "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q3.) **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)**

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: two hand-picked plays, one outcome each, no distribution of values, and no check that the model's read of "who failed" matches film beyond the speaker's statement that it "correctly" identified them (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [04:31]). The 10 to 15 versus 60 to 80 percent line shares are unexplained and the captions for both ranges are garbled, so the exact figures may differ. A single play is not evidence of accuracy.

**Example** — This entry is the example; see the two plays above.

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]; [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]]. Contrast with the pass-rush side example in [[principle--credit-pass-rush-pressure-throughout-the-play]] (SSAC24).

# CLIP Is Said to Beat Other Methods at Finding Top Linemen and Ranking by Salary

**What it is** — Jenkins reports three external comparisons (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [06:33], [07:03], [07:34]):

1. The causal model was "significantly better" at identifying top offensive linemen as indicated by All-Pro and Pro Bowl honors, shown as dark green shading in a chart.
2. It was "significantly better" in ranking players by salary, "much more consistent".
3. Aggregated on the 2023 Big Data Bowl sample, there is a "strong positive correlation" with Pro Football Focus rankings, with differences he attributes to PFF having the entire data set while his team had the first eight weeks of the 2020 to 2021 season (caption "2020 2021").

He adds that the model correlates strongly with completion percentage on individual plays, so teams with better lines complete more passes and win more games over a season (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism and no numbers: "significantly" has no test statistic, no correlation coefficient and no sample size in the talk. Inference: agreement with honors, salary and PFF shows the metric resembles consensus judgment, which is not evidence that the credit is causal.

**When to apply** — As an example of what external validation a vendor presents. Ask for the correlation values, the sample, what happens when honors and salary are held out, and whether the model finds linemen the consensus misses (the question that matters for recruiting, Inference).

Eric's baseline: "Data collection has a cost in time, athlete compliance, and staff attention. When the insight stops justifying that cost, it's time to stop collecting." (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-19). Inference: a method that mostly reproduces PFF rankings adds cost without new insight unless it disagrees with them usefully, and the talk does not show that.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked untested: no numbers back "significantly better", and honors and salary are shaped by the same reputation the model is compared with. The sample is eight weeks of one NFL season. The speaker is from the company that built the method. Do not use this entry to claim CLIP is more accurate than PFF grades.

**Example** — The comparison with PFF rankings on the 2023 Big Data Bowl sample, differing partly because PFF had the full season (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:03]).

**Related** — [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]]; [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[principle--player-credit-is-a-causal-question-not-a-prediction-residual]].

# Robustness Checks for a Causal Estimate: Balance, Placebo, Subsets, Sensitivity, Calibration

**What it is** — Jenkins says that with causal inference "you need to be able to run tests" to see how sensitive the result is to the assumptions (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]). The checks he reports for CLIP (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05], [08:35]):

1. **Covariate balance:** standardized mean differences "less than 0.1 after weighting", which he calls ideal.
2. **Placebo test:** replace the treatment with a placebo variable; the effect went to zero, which he says confirms the effect "is not due to chance". Inference: a placebo test checks for a spurious, method-made effect, not for sampling chance.
3. **Random-subset consistency:** CATE values stayed consistent across random subsets of the data.
4. **Sensitivity analysis:** add unobserved confounding variables in simulation; CATE values varied by "less than a 3% variation".
5. **Calibration and AUC curves** for the propensity model, since it is used to predict probabilities.

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that if the causal effect is real, the estimate should remain stable across subsets and vanish when the treatment is swapped for a placebo (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]). He gives no mechanism for the sensitivity threshold. Inference: covariate balance after weighting is the direct check that the propensity model did its job of making treated and untreated plays comparable on the measured features.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a causal or "adjusted" player metric from observational data: ask for balance after weighting, a placebo or negative-control test, stability across subsets, and a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounders. Inference: the same checklist applies to any claim that a training exposure caused a monitoring change.

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, Eric-authored Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: robustness checks are the model-side version of that standard.

**When NOT to apply** — The reported figures are the speaker's, from a talk with no table, no play or player counts, no confidence intervals, and no definition of how the 3 percent variation was measured (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:35]). The simulated confounders are ones he chose, so passing the sensitivity check is not proof that no real unmeasured confounder (for example scheme, play design or quarterback skill, Inference) is missing. The checks do not show that the player-level credit is right, only that the aggregate estimate is stable.

**Example** — The placebo check: swapping in a placebo treatment sent the effect to zero (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]).

**Related** — [[framework--clip-doubly-robust-outcome-and-propensity-models]]; [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]; calibration of a different model: [[heuristic--choose-a-calibrated-random-forest-for-a-continuous-probability-score]] and [[framework--deepqb-checking-outcome-predictions-by-calibration-and-split]].

# CLIP: A Doubly Robust Estimate of What Allowing Pressure Does to Completion

**What it is** — CLIP (caption: "causal impact of offensive alignment on pass plays", while the video title says "Offensive Linemen"; pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:30]) estimates how pressure allowed by an offensive lineman changes completion probability, per lineman, per play, every tenth of a second (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [01:30], [04:31]). Two models (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:01], [10:35]):

1. **Outcome model:** probability of a completed pass from features X and whether pressure was allowed.
2. **Propensity score model:** probability that the lineman allows pressure, from features X. Inverse propensity weighting uses it to build a more balanced data set for comparing outcomes (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [10:35]).

The estimator is called doubly robust because "it only requires one of the two models to be correctly specified" to identify the causal effect (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:01]). The captions name it "a w robust estimator" (garbled; the name is not confirmed here). The target is the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) per player per play: expected completion given pressure occurred minus expected completion given it did not, given features X (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [03:31]). # Robustness Checks for a Causal Estimate: Balance, Placebo, Subsets, Sensitivity, Calibration

**What it is** — Jenkins says that with causal inference "you need to be able to run tests" to see how sensitive the result is to the assumptions (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [07:34]). The checks he reports for CLIP (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05], [08:35]):

1. **Covariate balance:** standardized mean differences "less than 0.1 after weighting", which he calls ideal.
2. **Placebo test:** replace the treatment with a placebo variable; the effect went to zero, which he says confirms the effect "is not due to chance". Inference: a placebo test checks for a spurious, method-made effect, not for sampling chance.
3. **Random-subset consistency:** CATE values stayed consistent across random subsets of the data.
4. **Sensitivity analysis:** add unobserved confounding variables in simulation; CATE values varied by "less than a 3% variation".
5. **Calibration and AUC curves** for the propensity model, since it is used to predict probabilities.

**Why it works** — The speaker's reasoning is that if the causal effect is real, the estimate should remain stable across subsets and vanish when the treatment is swapped for a placebo (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]). He gives no mechanism for the sensitivity threshold. Inference: covariate balance after weighting is the direct check that the propensity model did its job of making treated and untreated plays comparable on the measured features.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a causal or "adjusted" player metric from observational data: ask for balance after weighting, a placebo or negative-control test, stability across subsets, and a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounders. Inference: the same checklist applies to any claim that a training exposure caused a monitoring change.

Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, Eric-authored Nordbord piece, in method-baseline.md). Inference: robustness checks are the model-side version of that standard.

**When NOT to apply** — The reported figures are the speaker's, from a talk with no table, no play or player counts, no confidence intervals, and no definition of how the 3 percent variation was measured (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:35]). The simulated confounders are ones he chose, so passing the sensitivity check is not proof that no real unmeasured confounder (for example scheme, play design or quarterback skill, Inference) is missing. The checks do not show that the player-level credit is right, only that the aggregate estimate is stable.

**Example** — The placebo check: swapping in a placebo treatment sent the effect to zero (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [08:05]).

[00:00]
Hello everybody. My name is Ben Jenkins.
I'm a PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic
University. I'm excited to share our
work on how we can apply causal modeling
to be able to better estimate the impact
of defensive players on tackling plays.
The NFL in football in general has a
defensive attribution problem. What I
mean by that is we see on this left
figure, this is a it's a running play
where the ball carrier is in yellow and
he gets tackled behind the line of
scrimmage and this results in a 6-yard
loss. And the question is who gets
credit for this play? All right, so we
have the defenses in red and traditional

[00:31]
metrics would only credit the tackler
with the play. The reality is that
there's multiple defenders on this play
who contributed causally to the outcome.
Defensive value is largely invisible in
traditional metrics and coordination and
positioning matter much more than just
the final contact. We want to use the
tracking data NFL tracking data from the
2024 NFL Big Data Bowl to answer
counterfactual or what if questions.
That is, what would happen without this
defender or without this defender's
contribution?
Uh a typical approach in in order to

[01:01]
estimate the value of a player on a play
is a supervised learning. So they build
a model that's going to ask what will
happen. So it's mainly prediction
focused. So for example, given player
positions, you can break some outcome.
For example, what's the expected points
added on the play.
It's correlation-based. So the goal is
to find patterns in the data and the
goal is to minimize some prediction
error. Some typical problems that we see

-**When NOT to apply** — Marked contested. The talk is a method presentation by its builder (Sumer Sports), and its causal reading depends on assumptions the talk checks only partly (see [[framework--causal-model-robustness-checks-balance-placebo-sensitivity]]). The DeepQB talk (EeBgUCYhezc [12:23]) and the residual metrics the speaker names (rush yards over expected, completion percentage over expected, [09:05]) treat the residual as credit; this talk disagrees with that approach, and the library does not hold evidence that settles it. Inference: residual metrics and causal estimates answer different questions (how a player compares with typical, versus what a player's action did), and both can be useful for a screening or scouting decision, so the principle should not be read as "residuals are wrong". The talk also says residual metrics "are useful" (pcp9h_M6Ir8 [09:05]). Validation shown is against honors, salary and PFF, which agree with consensus and are not themselves a test of cause (see [[claim--clip-validation-against-honors-salary-and-pff]]).

# Case Study: One Play and Aaron Donald Under Expected Points Saved

**What it is** — Two worked examples from Ben Jenkins's talk.

**The 6-yard-loss play.** A running play where the ball carrier is tackled behind the line for a 6-yard loss (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00]). Traditional metrics credit only the tackler (JHgeEo3n1do [00:31]). Under the speaker's model the tackler has the highest value, and "four other players" also contribute positively. The speaker reads this as the model capturing coordinated effort and identifying "setup players who are largely invisible in traditional metrics" (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). The captions do not show the values.

**Aaron Donald.** The speaker compares the distribution of EPA when Donald makes a tackle with the distribution when he does not, and takes the difference as his expected points saved. The captions describe the orange and blue distributions inconsistently, so which is tackle and which is no tackle is unclear (JHgeEo3n1do [06:40]). His EPS "is around 0.27, meaning each Donald tackle prevents around 0.27 expected points for the offense" (JHgeEo3n1do [06:40], [07:09]). In Q&A he says Donald in the backfield who forces the ball carrier elsewhere gets positive credit, and on a pass play he can reduce the odds the pass is beneficial (JHgeEo3n1do [11:13]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's interpretation is that the tackle effect is the gap between the two EPA distributions (JHgeEo3n1do [06:40]). The talk offers no independent confirmation that 0.27 is correct. Inference: with no known true effect (the speaker notes real causal effects are not observable, JHgeEo3n1do [08:10]), a single player's number is a model output, not a measured fact.

**When to apply** — Use as a template for reading a per-player "value per event" figure: ask what the event is, what the comparison is, and what the distributions look like before reading the difference. Inference: for Baylor, a per-event figure from any vendor deserves the same questions.

The Donald figure is for an NFL defensive tackle on NFL tracking data and has no meaning for another level of play. The Q&A answer on pass plays and disruption without a tackle is general, and the captions give no values (JHgeEo3n1do [11:13]).

confidence: untested

# Defenders Are Not Independent: 68 Percent of Plays Show Interference

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins says traditional methods assume each defender acts independently, which "violates the reality" (JHgeEo3n1do [02:31], [03:01]). He names three interactions that break independence and must be modeled jointly (JHgeEo3n1do [03:01], [03:31]):
- **Coordination:** two players working together to make a tackle.
- **Interference:** one defender's action changes the best action of another. His example: the defensive end sets the edge, which lets a linebacker make the tackle.
- **Substitution effects:** one defender's poor play on a snap changes what the other defender has to do.

His reported result: "68% of plays show these significant interference effects," and modeling them gives a "significant bias reduction" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40], [09:10]). He describes football defense as an adaptive system where individual value comes from group behavior, likening it to a flock of birds (JHgeEo3n1do [03:31]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's mechanism is the coordination structure of a defense: one defender's movement changes the best actions for his teammates (JHgeEo3n1do [02:31]). He does not say how interference is measured or what "significant" means for each play. Inference: if a set-up defender's contribution shows up only through a teammate's tackle, any per-player metric that ignores the link will push his credit onto the teammate.

**When to apply** — As a warning label on any individual defensive metric (tackles, pressures, stops): ask whether the number sits on the last player in a chain. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q3): "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (Explicit). Inference: a per-player defensive number is a good candidate for that test when the question is "who caused this".

**When NOT to apply** — The 68% figure comes from one proof-of-concept dataset, the first 9 weeks of the 2022 NFL regular season (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). The talk does not say how "significant" was tested, whether the figure is per defender or per play across the whole defense, or how it varies by scheme. The model-versus-supervised comparison (R-squared, RMSE) uses synthetic data because the real data has no known causal effect, and the speaker also cites salary and Pro Bowl rankings (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10], [08:40]); how the bias reduction itself was measured is not described. `untested`. Do not read it as a rate for college or for any single scheme.

**Example** — The speaker's: a defensive end sets the edge so a linebacker can make the tackle (JHgeEo3n1do [03:01]). Inference: the point of modeling interference jointly is that an edge setter who makes no tackle can still get credit; the speaker does not show an edge-setter result (the worked tackle example is [[case-study--one-play-and-aaron-donald-expected-points-saved]]).

**Related** — [[framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting]], [[principle--prediction-is-not-attribution-in-defensive-evaluation]].

confidence: untested

# Scheme Is a Confounder the Model Only Partly Handles

**What it is** — In Q&A a questioner points out that a blitzing linebacker has a much higher probability of being in a high-EPA play than a linebacker who is dropping into coverage, so scheme could confound the metric, and the data did not include play calls (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43], [12:13]). A speaker replies (the talk is introduced by Ben Jenkins, but the Q&A captions carry no speaker labels) that knowing the scheme and each player's responsibility on the play is ongoing research, and that one way the model partly captures it is propensity weighting: if a defender has a very low chance of being involved and makes a tackle, that play gets higher weight, which reduces some of the bias. With scheme data the answer says the estimates would improve quite a bit (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13], [12:43]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's claim is that the propensity score absorbs how likely a defender is to be involved, which scheme partly determines (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]). The talk does not show that the propensity model recovers assignments. Inference: the weighting can only correct for scheme to the extent the tracking features (positions, speeds, directions) reveal it before the tackle, so an assignment that looks the same as another cannot be separated.

**When to apply** — As the first question to ask of any defender-level number: which players' roles make the event more likely? Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q6): the coach's eye "can direct you where to look and gather data to investigate further" (Explicit). Inference: staff who know the call and assignment hold exactly the context missing from the data; a number is a prompt to ask them, not the verdict.

**When NOT to apply** — The answer is partial and general: the captions give no test of how much scheme bias remains (JHgeEo3n1do [12:43]). `untested`: an assertion in response to a question, not a reported result. Do not read it as "scheme is handled".

**Example** — The questioner's: a blitzing linebacker versus a dropping one (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43]). The speaker's partial answer: low-probability tackler gets more weight (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]).

confidence: untested

# Expected Points Saved: Tackle as Treatment, EPA as Outcome, Propensity Weighting

**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, frames defender credit as a treatment effect (JHgeEo3n1do [04:02]).
- **Treatment:** a binary indicator that the defender made the tackle on the play.
- **Outcome:** expected points added (EPA), the traditional NFL metric of how much the offense benefits.
- **Expected points saved (EPS):** expected EPA on the play if the defender did not make the tackle, minus expected EPA if he did (JHgeEo3n1do [04:02], [04:33]).
- **Architecture:** a transformer that processes all 22 players at once; the speaker says its attention mechanism captures defender coordination and interference effects (JHgeEo3n1do [04:33]).
- **Inputs (shown on a causal graph, DAG):** each defender's x-y position, speed and direction; the same for the ball carrier; relational features (defender relative to ball carrier); the 10 teammates of each defender; opponents; game context (JHgeEo3n1do [04:33], [05:04]).
- **Two models:** a propensity score model (probability a defender makes a tackle given all tracking information) and an outcome model (expected EPA with and without that defender's tackle) (JHgeEo3n1do [05:04], [05:35]).
- **Weighting:** inverse propensity weighting to build a "pseudo population" in which tackle involvement is independent of context and "effectively randomized" (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]).
- **Doubly robust estimation:** named at the close as protection "against model misspecification" (JHgeEo3n1do [09:41]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated logic is that reweighting by the inverse of the probability of being involved removes the context that made involvement likely (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]), and a low-probability defender who makes a tackle gets higher weight (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]). He gives no proof or diagnostic that the propensity model balances the groups. Inference: the estimate is only as good as the propensity model, which the talk does not show being checked.

**When to apply** — As a recipe for any "who deserves credit" question where several people act on one outcome: define the treatment, define the outcome, model who gets the treatment, then reweight. Eric's baseline: none found. method-baseline.md holds no position on causal inference or counterfactual models. Inference: Baylor lacks league-wide tracking data for this exact build, so the lasting use is the design logic (treatment, outcome, propensity, weighting) when judging an outside metric someone brings to Applied Performance.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker calls it a proof of concept on the first 9 weeks of the 2022 NFL regular season (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). The captions do not say how many plays per defender, how the propensity model was checked, or how the "treatment" is defined for players who get credit without tackling (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). The video description names adversarial representation balancing, Bayesian uncertainty and sensitivity analyses, but none is described in the talk (JHgeEo3n1do meta.json description, not in the talk). A questioner points out that scheme and assignment are not in the data, and the speaker says it is ongoing research (JHgeEo3n1do [11:43], [12:13], [12:43]). `untested`: the captions give few validation values (about 41 percent of variance in tackle-play outcomes explained at team level, [08:10]; higher R-squared and lower RMSE than supervised models, with no values captioned, [08:40]); no check of the propensity model is described.

**Example** — The speaker's example play: the tackler scores highest and four other defenders get positive value (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). See [[case-study--one-play-and-aaron-donald-expected-points-saved]].

**Related** — [[principle--prediction-is-not-attribution-in-defensive-evaluation]], [[framework--validating-a-causal-metric-with-no-ground-truth]], [[claim--defender-interference-in-68-percent-of-plays]], [[claim--scheme-confound-is-only-partly-handled-by-propensity-weighting]].
=================== framework--validating-a-causal-metric-with-no-ground-truth.md
confidence: untested

# Validating a Causal Metric When the True Effect Cannot Be Observed

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins notes that with observational data "we don't have the underlying causal effect" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10], [08:40]), so he checks the metric indirectly (JHgeEo3n1do [07:09] to [09:10]):
1. **Face validity against honors:** top-10 rankings by position (defensive end, defensive tackle, outside and inside linebacker), with All-Pro and Pro Bowl players marked; he reports a "much better correlation" than supervised models (JHgeEo3n1do [07:09], [07:39]).
2. **Team-level aggregation:** mean individual EPS plotted against mean individual EPA for tacklers shows a strong negative correlation, which he says helps explain 41% of the variance in tackle play outcomes (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39], [08:10]).
3. **Synthetic data:** against independent models, his model has "significantly higher R-squared" and "much lower RMSE"; no values are given (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]).
4. **Salary rank:** better ranking of non-rookie players by salary and by Pro Bowl status (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's argument is that individual causal estimates that aggregate to team results and match honors are capturing "some of the genuine defensive value, not just the statistical artifacts" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10]). The talk does not say why salary and honors should be unbiased proxies. Inference: honors and salaries are themselves partly produced by tackle counts, the quantity he criticizes, so agreement with them is weak evidence.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a model with no ground truth: ask what the synthetic-data test knew that the model did not, what outside labels were used, and whether those labels share the model's bias. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a) uses "standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" for individualized thresholds (Explicit). Inference: that is a within-athlete noise check; the checks above are between-player, a different question.

**When NOT to apply** — Only the 41% and 68% figures are given as numbers. R-squared, RMSE, rank correlations and salary comparisons are stated as better with no values (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]). `untested`. Validation is by synthetic data and honors, not by a known true effect, and the speaker's claims of being first and of better ranking are his own in a competition presentation. Not a recipe for non-NFL data.

**Example** — The speaker's: the team-level plot, where better-tackler teams (higher mean EPS) tend to allow better outcomes, 41% of variance (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39], [08:10]).

**Related** — [[framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting]], [[heuristic--year-to-year-stability-as-test-of-real-skill]], a different validity check on the ESPN receiver metric.
=================== principle--prediction-is-not-attribution-in-defensive-evaluation.md
confidence: untested

# Prediction Is Not Attribution in Defensive Evaluation

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins (PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic University, as introduced in the first lines) argues that football has a "defensive attribution problem" (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00]). On a running play tackled for a 6-yard loss, traditional metrics credit only the tackler, though several defenders contributed (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00], [00:31]). The speaker contrasts two model types. A supervised model asks what will happen, is correlation-based, minimizes prediction error, and in the speaker's words "often confuses correlation with causation," is biased toward high-volume tacklers, and struggles to separate skill from opportunity (JHgeEo3n1do [01:01], [01:31]). A causal model asks what would happen if the defender had not made the tackle, which the speaker says isolates individual contributions, accounts for situational context, and separates player effect from team and scheme effects (JHgeEo3n1do [01:31], [02:01]). The speaker's bottom line is that prediction is different from attribution (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives one reason for the contrast: a predictive model optimizes error loss, not an estimate of one player's contribution (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]). The speaker gives no further mechanism for why high-volume tacklers are favored. Inference: a defender who is often near the ball will correlate with good outcomes whether or not he caused them, and a loss function that only rewards prediction accuracy has no reason to separate the two.

**When to apply** — When a number is going to be read as "this player caused this result" (contract, grade, or scheme decisions, which the speaker lists as uses at JHgeEo3n1do [10:11]) and the underlying model was fit only to predict an outcome. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12) says ACWR is "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally" (Explicit). Inference: that is the same worry, a summary number read as if it explained something. Ask of any Baylor metric whether it was built to predict or to attribute.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker lists the limits of the causal side: it "requires a larger set of assumptions," needs more quality control, and cannot be applied in every scenario (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]). The comparison with supervised models is the speaker's own; no head-to-head numbers appear in the captions beyond "better correlation" with honors (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39]). The data are NFL tracking data (the speaker names the 2024 NFL Big Data Bowl, JHgeEo3n1do [00:31]) for the first 9 weeks of the 2022 regular season, and the speaker calls the work a proof of concept (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). It is an assertion from a competition presentation, not a validated finding, hence `untested`. It does not transfer to college or Baylor data without a tracking source.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 6-yard-loss run, where the tackler gets the credit and, in the speaker's model, four other defenders also receive positive value (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). See [[case-study--one-play-and-aaron-donald-expected-points-saved]].

**Related** — [[framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting]], the model built on this premise. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]], a library framework on separating raw output from its interpretation. [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]], the ESPN talk faces a similar credit problem for receivers (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:18]); a panelist there says the nearest-defender version of defender credit "just isn't immediately clear" in zone coverage (teg9SfzpMy0 [44:15]).

- **Two models:** a propensity score model (probability a defender makes a tackle given all tracking information) and an outcome model (expected EPA with and without that defender's tackle) (JHgeEo3n1do [05:04], [05:35]).
- **Weighting:** inverse propensity weighting to build a "pseudo population" in which tackle involvement is independent of context and "effectively randomized" (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]).
- **Doubly robust estimation:** named at the close as protection "against model misspecification" (JHgeEo3n1do [09:41]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's stated logic is that reweighting by the inverse of the probability of being involved removes the context that made involvement likely (JHgeEo3n1do [05:35]), and a low-probability defender who makes a tackle gets higher weight (JHgeEo3n1do [12:13]). Inference: Baylor lacks league-wide tracking data for this exact build, so the lasting use is the design logic (treatment, outcome, propensity, weighting) when judging an outside metric someone brings to Applied Performance.

# Validating a Causal Metric When the True Effect Cannot Be Observed

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins notes that with observational data "we don't have the underlying causal effect" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10], [08:40]), so he checks the metric indirectly (JHgeEo3n1do [07:09] to [09:10]):
1. **Face validity against honors:** top-10 rankings by position (defensive end, defensive tackle, outside and inside linebacker), with All-Pro and Pro Bowl players marked; he reports a "much better correlation" than supervised models (JHgeEo3n1do [07:09], [07:39]).
2. **Team-level aggregation:** mean individual EPS plotted against mean individual EPA for tacklers shows a strong negative correlation, which he says helps explain 41% of the variance in tackle play outcomes (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39], [08:10]).
3. **Synthetic data:** against independent models, his model has "significantly higher R-squared" and "much lower RMSE"; no values are given (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]).
4. **Salary rank:** better ranking of non-rookie players by salary and by Pro Bowl status (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's argument is that individual causal estimates that aggregate to team results and match honors are capturing "some of the genuine defensive value, not just the statistical artifacts" (JHgeEo3n1do [08:10]). The talk does not say why salary and honors should be unbiased proxies. Inference: honors and salaries are themselves partly produced by tackle counts, the quantity he criticizes, so agreement with them is weak evidence.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when someone presents a model with no ground truth: ask what the synthetic-data test knew that the model did not, what outside labels were used, and whether those labels share the model's bias. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q2a) uses "standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" for individualized thresholds (Explicit). Inference: that is a within-athlete noise check; the checks above are between-player, a different question.

**When NOT to apply** — Only the 41% and 68% figures are given as numbers. R-squared, RMSE, rank correlations and salary comparisons are stated as better with no values (JHgeEo3n1do [08:40]). `untested`. Validation is by synthetic data and honors, not by a known true effect, and the speaker's claims of being first and of better ranking are his own in a competition presentation. Not a recipe for non-NFL data.

**Example** — The speaker's: the team-level plot, where better-tackler teams (higher mean EPS) tend to allow better outcomes, 41% of variance (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39], [08:10]).

# Prediction Is Not Attribution in Defensive Evaluation

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins (PhD candidate at Florida Atlantic University, as introduced in the first lines) argues that football has a "defensive attribution problem" (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00]). On a running play tackled for a 6-yard loss, traditional metrics credit only the tackler, though several defenders contributed (JHgeEo3n1do [00:00], [00:31]). The speaker contrasts two model types. A supervised model asks what will happen, is correlation-based, minimizes prediction error, and in the speaker's words "often confuses correlation with causation," is biased toward high-volume tacklers, and struggles to separate skill from opportunity (JHgeEo3n1do [01:01], [01:31]). A causal model asks what would happen if the defender had not made the tackle, which the speaker says isolates individual contributions, accounts for situational context, and separates player effect from team and scheme effects (JHgeEo3n1do [01:31], [02:01]). The speaker's bottom line is that prediction is different from attribution (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives one reason for the contrast: a predictive model optimizes error loss, not an estimate of one player's contribution (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]). The speaker gives no further mechanism for why high-volume tacklers are favored. Inference: a defender who is often near the ball will correlate with good outcomes whether or not he caused them, and a loss function that only rewards prediction accuracy has no reason to separate the two.

**When to apply** — When a number is going to be read as "this player caused this result" (contract, grade, or scheme decisions, which the speaker lists as uses at JHgeEo3n1do [10:11]) and the underlying model was fit only to predict an outcome. Eric's baseline: Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q12) says ACWR is "raw, has error, is misleading, and lacks context generally" (Explicit). Inference: that is the same worry, a summary number read as if it explained something. Ask of any Baylor metric whether it was built to predict or to attribute.

**When NOT to apply** — The speaker lists the limits of the causal side: it "requires a larger set of assumptions," needs more quality control, and cannot be applied in every scenario (JHgeEo3n1do [02:01]). The comparison with supervised models is the speaker's own; no head-to-head numbers appear in the captions beyond "better correlation" with honors (JHgeEo3n1do [07:39]). The data are NFL tracking data (the speaker names the 2024 NFL Big Data Bowl, JHgeEo3n1do [00:31]) for the first 9 weeks of the 2022 regular season, and the speaker calls the work a proof of concept (JHgeEo3n1do [09:10]). It is an assertion from a competition presentation, not a validated finding, hence `untested`. It does not transfer to college or Baylor data without a tracking source.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the 6-yard-loss run, where the tackler gets the credit and, in the speaker's model, four other defenders also receive positive value (JHgeEo3n1do [06:08]). See [[case-study--one-play-and-aaron-donald-expected-points-saved]].

**Related** — [[framework--expected-points-saved-treatment-outcome-and-propensity-weighting]], the model built on this premise. [[framework--measurement-versus-inference]], a library framework on separating raw output from its interpretation. [[framework--receiver-creates-own-context-general-plus-specific-estimates]], the ESPN talk faces a similar credit problem for receivers (teg9SfzpMy0 [25:18]); a panelist there says the nearest-defender version of defender credit "just isn't immediately clear" in zone coverage (teg9SfzpMy0 [44:15]).
