=================== case-study--gobert-defensive-value-box-score-misses.md
confidence: untested

# Case study: Rudy Gobert ranks 54th on traditional metrics and 12th on the model

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins decomposes player value by source. Nikola Jokic ranks first in the top 15 and excels at playmaking, scoring and defensive rebounding; Stephen Curry scores very well and is weaker on defense; Rudy Gobert's value is "largely defensive presence and defensive actions" (JjeFktc4QLM [08:09], [08:40], [09:10]). The speaker says Gobert is traditionally ranked 54th, the model has him 12th, and "the box score missed 45% of his defensive value", which he links to opponents scoring less and getting fewer paint opportunities when Gobert is on the floor (JjeFktc4QLM [09:10]). He also reports substantial agreement with RAPM and worse agreement with box plus-minus, which he ties to defensive valuation (JjeFktc4QLM [08:09], [08:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is that defensive value comes from presence and deterrence, not countable actions, and the model credits presence (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07], [09:10]). The captions show no independent check of the defensive value (Inference: the same model produced both the ranking and the 45% figure).

**When to apply** — As a template for checking where a model and a box-score metric disagree: decompose the player's value by source, then ask whether the disagreement lies where the simple metric is blind. Inference: in football, where PFF defensive grades and counting stats diverge for a defender, use film to see whether the gap is coverage or pressure value the counting stats miss.

**When NOT to apply** — A single player, one model, one season of ranking, with no uncertainty shown, so confidence is untested. The 45% and the 54th-versus-12th figures are as spoken and could not be checked against a chart in the captions. Do not treat one disagreement as evidence that defensive specialists are broadly undervalued in markets; the speaker states that as his view (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40]) and the talk shows no market test. Do not apply to football without a football defensive-presence model.

**Example** — The case is itself the example: Gobert 54th traditional, 12th by the model (JjeFktc4QLM [09:10]).

**Related** — [[claim--synergy-and-fit-effects-from-drl-shapley]], [[framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation]].
=================== claim--drl-shapley-predicts-games-better-than-box-metrics-but-not-vegas.md
confidence: untested

# Adding the model improves game prediction over traditional metrics, but the Vegas line stays best

**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, tests how well the model predicts games on out-of-sample data, against a Vegas line benchmark. The speaker reports that the Vegas line alone "is obviously the best, has the highest win prediction"; adding the deep RL Shapley values improves over the traditional metrics, and adding the synergy effects improves accuracy further, getting closer to the Vegas line (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42], [12:12]). The speaker concludes the learned values "capture real forward-looking predictive signals" (JjeFktc4QLM [12:12]). The accuracy figures are shown only on a chart and are not stated in the captions, so no effect size can be cited here (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). The validation sums the players' Shapley values on the court to predict games, which a judge questioned (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [13:44]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism beyond the value being learned from outcomes and including interaction. Inference: a benchmark that already prices public information (the Vegas line) is a hard test, so falling short of it is the expected result for a player-value model rather than a failure.

**When to apply** — As a model for how to validate a player-value metric: hold out data, compare against an existing predictive benchmark, and add the new metric to it rather than replacing it. Inference: a football grade or load metric could be tested the same way against a simple baseline on held-out games.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: an out-of-sample comparison against named benchmarks is described, but no accuracy numbers, no uncertainty and no data split appear in the captions, and the speaker's own chart is the only result. In the Q&A the speaker says the data are about five seasons of NBA play-by-play, "thousands of games" (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]). Do not read this as beating the market: the Vegas line was best (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). Do not assume a similar gain for a football metric.

**Example** — The speaker's own ladder: Vegas line alone, then adding the model's values, then adding synergy, each step closer to the Vegas line (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42], [12:12]).

**Related** — [[claim--synergy-and-fit-effects-from-drl-shapley]], [[claim--drl-shapley-stabilizes-faster-than-rapm]], [[framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout]].
=================== claim--drl-shapley-stabilizes-faster-than-rapm.md
confidence: untested

# The speaker's model stabilizes player values faster than regularized adjusted plus-minus

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins says regularized adjusted plus-minus (RAPM) needs a large sample to converge, and that his rankings need "around 67% fewer possessions to achieve similar comparable accuracy" (JjeFktc4QLM [06:38]). He also says the deep RL Shapley method "takes around 3 weeks to stabilize compared to 2 months" for RAPM (JjeFktc4QLM [07:08]). The two figures are stated separately and he does not link them. Inference: they are roughly consistent, since 3 weeks is about 65% fewer than 2 months (about 8.7 weeks). Why it matters, in his words: teams constantly weigh acquiring a role player, and identifying underlying ability sooner supports better decisions (JjeFktc4QLM [06:38], [07:08]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism in the captions. Inference: a model that uses game state and sequence may extract more information per possession than a regression on who is on the floor, but the talk does not say so.

**When to apply** — As a reason to ask how many possessions, games or weeks a metric needs before it is stable. Inference: Baylor could write a rule for how many games or test weeks a transfer or early-enrolled player needs before his grade moves a recruiting or playing-time decision, and test it on past seasons. Eric's baseline: no direct position on valuation-model stabilization (method-baseline.md).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: the captions give no definition of "stabilize", no comparison design, no player-level confidence intervals and no accuracy numbers for the stabilization comparison. The benchmark is RAPM on NBA data, and a one-college-season football sample is far smaller (Inference). Do not adopt the 3-week figure as a Baylor waiting period.

**Example** — The speaker's own statement of the comparison: about 3 weeks versus 2 months (JjeFktc4QLM [07:08]). No worked player example is given.

**Related** — [[framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation]], [[claim--drl-shapley-predicts-games-better-than-box-metrics-but-not-vegas]].
=================== claim--synergy-and-fit-effects-from-drl-shapley.md
confidence: untested

# Player values are not additive: 89 synergies, 61 anti-synergies, and a five-win fit claim

**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, measures synergy by comparing how pairs perform together on the court versus off it, shown in a two-way quadrant plot: upper right is two-way synergy (better on offense and defense together), lower left is two-way anti-synergy (worse on both) (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40], [10:10]). He reports 89 positive synergies and 61 anti-synergies (JjeFktc4QLM [10:10]). He argues traditional metrics assume additivity: two players each at plus two per 100 possessions are assumed to give plus four, which "doesn't actually happen in reality" (JjeFktc4QLM [10:10], [10:41]). Adding synergy explains some of the "win residual" (actual results minus the model's prediction) (JjeFktc4QLM [11:11]). His headline: "two equally talented rosters can differ five plus wins solely based on their fit" (JjeFktc4QLM [11:11], [12:43]). For Rudy Gobert-type defenders he says a team of scorers around them matters, and that defensive specialists are undervalued by traditional metrics, which he calls a potential competitive advantage (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's explanation is complementarity: spacing, screens and rotations make one player's value depend on teammates, and deterrence on defense does not show up in box scores (JjeFktc4QLM [05:38]). The five-win figure is reported without how it was computed (JjeFktc4QLM [11:11]).

**When to apply** — As a prompt to check whether a unit's results differ from the sum of its parts. Inference: for the offensive line, compare five-man combinations that played together against a simple sum of per-player PFF grades. When PFF defensive grades and counting stats disagree for a player, treat the gap as a question for film, not a tie-break (Inference). Eric's baseline: no direct position on synergy or player-fit models (method-baseline.md).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested: all figures are from NBA data with no uncertainty shown, and the 89 and 61 counts carry no definition of a threshold in the captions. A judge's portability objection to Shapley values (see [[framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout]]) applies directly, and a questioner raised that pairs who almost always play together (example in the captions: Jokic and Murray) give few samples; the speaker replied that five seasons of play-by-play data make sample size "not too much of a problem," except for new players, where extrapolation is more limited (JjeFktc4QLM [15:49], [16:21]). The "market inefficiency" and trade-fit claims are the author's view (JjeFktc4QLM [09:40], [10:41]). College rosters turn over yearly and units are larger, so NBA pair results do not transfer to line continuity without checking (Inference).

**Example** — The speaker's additivity example: two players at plus two points per 100 possessions assumed to sum to plus four (JjeFktc4QLM [10:10]).

**Related** — [[framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout]], [[case-study--gobert-defensive-value-box-score-misses]], [[claim--drl-shapley-predicts-games-better-than-box-metrics-but-not-vegas]].
=================== framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation.md
confidence: untested

# Valuing actions with a Markov decision process and an advantage function

**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, frames basketball as a Markov decision process: a current state, an action taken, a stochastic transition, and an immediate reward measured both in expected points and in change in win probability (JjeFktc4QLM [04:05]). The key quantity is an advantage function: the expected value of an action beyond the baseline state expectation, which makes the valuation context-aware (JjeFktc4QLM [04:35]). Credit is split in two ways.
- **On-ball offense** (shots, assists, turnovers): valued by action type, player role and game context (JjeFktc4QLM [04:35], [05:07]).
- **Defense and off-ball influence**: valued by presence and constraints, not individual actions, to capture deterrence unseen in box scores (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07]).
The speaker positions it against three earlier families: box-score metrics (PER, win shares, box plus-minus: fixed weights, overweight scoring, weak on defense, no context), adjusted and regularized adjusted plus-minus (RAPM: regress possession outcomes on who is on the floor, but assume context-invariant contributions and miss synergy), and sequential models such as expected possession value (capture flow but struggle to credit players) (JjeFktc4QLM [01:01], [01:31], [02:02], [02:32]). The video description also names temporal-difference learning and a distributional win-probability model; the captions do not describe them. One caption spelling, "DRPM", appears for the model's name (JjeFktc4QLM [15:49]).

**Why it works** — The speaker says deep reinforcement learning can combine the strength of sequential models (context and the flow of play) with player-level credit (JjeFktc4QLM [02:02], [02:32]). The captions give no training details, so how well the learned values are calibrated is not stated.

**When to apply** — As a checklist for what a valuation model must handle: state, action, transition, reward, a baseline for "expected from this state", and a separate route for value that is not an action (defense, spacing). Inference: for football, ask the same questions of any grade or load number before comparing players. Eric's baseline: no direct position on valuation models (method-baseline.md).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested for this audience: the captions show no model specification, no calibration and no uncertainty for player values, and predictive accuracy is shown only on a chart (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). It was built on about five seasons of NBA play-by-play (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]); a football version needs its own state definition and a win-probability model, and none was shown. The defensive-value claims rest on the model with no independent check named.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a made three as the action, with reward measured as expected points on the play plus change in win probability (JjeFktc4QLM [04:05]).

**Related** — [[principle--identical-actions-carry-different-win-value-by-game-state]], [[framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout]], [[claim--drl-shapley-predicts-games-better-than-box-metrics-but-not-vegas]].
=================== framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout.md
confidence: contested

# Splitting team value among players with neural Shapley values, and the portability objection

**What it is** — The attribution problem: ten players interact on the court, so a simple credit system ignores context and interaction (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07], [05:38]). The speaker, Ben Jenkins, uses Shapley values to allocate total team value among players. Each player is replaced with a baseline embedding learned from the reinforcement-learning model, and the change in expected points and win probability is measured; this also exposes synergy, meaning teammates who perform better or worse together (JjeFktc4QLM [06:08]). Exact Shapley values are computationally heavy, so a neural approximation is used (JjeFktc4QLM [06:08], [06:38]). In the Q&A a questioner (a judge) objects that the Shapley values are contextual, not designed to be portable across lineups, yet validation sums them to predict games (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [13:44], [14:16]). The speaker agrees ("I think you're right about that") and proposes player dropout: instead of using dropout for regularization, swap each player for a neutral baseline embedding, measure the change in win prediction, and sum over the five on the court (JjeFktc4QLM [14:16], [14:46]). He says this was not in the paper and he expects a better estimate. A second questioner describes the method as averaging a player "across all combinations with a guy out of the lineup" and asks about two players who "platoon all the time" (JjeFktc4QLM [15:18]); the speaker answers that the model accounts for who is on the court and that five seasons of play-by-play limits the sample problem, though new players need extrapolation that is "a little bit limited" in accuracy (JjeFktc4QLM [15:19], [15:49], [16:21]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's case is that the baseline-embedding swap prices each player against a neutral replacement. The "averages over who is present" description is the second questioner's wording (JjeFktc4QLM [15:18]), not a mechanism the speaker states. The captions give no further mechanism, and the judge's objection is that this contextual value is then used as if context-free.

**When to apply** — When you must split a unit's result among its members and the members interact (a five-man group, a pairing). Inference: the portability objection means a player's Shapley value is best read as value within the lineups he played in, not a transferable rating.

**When NOT to apply** — Contested inside the talk: the judge's objection and the speaker's partial concession (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [14:16]) leave the portability problem open, and the proposed dropout fix is not validated in the captions. A questioner raised that pairs who nearly always play together give few samples; the speaker replied that with five seasons of play-by-play "the sample size isn't necessarily a problem," except for new players, where extrapolation is "a little bit limited" (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]). Both the concern and the reply are unvalidated in the captions. Inference: in college football, with 11 players per side and yearly turnover, a five-player Shapley split needs many more shared snaps than the talk's NBA data had, and none were checked.

**Example** — Raised in the Q&A exchange (attribution unclear at the speaker change): Jokic and Murray, who are usually on the court together (caption spelling), as the hard case for attribution (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]).

**Related** — [[claim--synergy-and-fit-effects-from-drl-shapley]], [[framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation]].
=================== principle--identical-actions-carry-different-win-value-by-game-state.md
confidence: untested

# The same recorded action is worth different amounts depending on game state

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins argues that winning is contextual: the same action has very different value depending on game state, teammates and opponents (JjeFktc4QLM [00:00], [00:31]). His example is a made three-pointer recorded identically in the box score: in the first quarter with the team up 15 it changed win probability by 2%; in the fourth quarter of a tied game with about a minute and 30 left it changed it by 23% (JjeFktc4QLM [03:03]). He calls this a "10 times difference"; Inference: 23 divided by 2 is about 11.5, so "10 times" is approximate as spoken. He says box-score metrics such as PER and box plus-minus treat the two shots as roughly the same and so "flatten player value", making role players in blowouts look as valuable as clutch performers (JjeFktc4QLM [03:03], [03:34]). Across action types, he reports that value is highest in close clutch games, where a three-pointer can be worth "more than double" its traditional value, and shrinks in blowouts, with offensive rebounds and steals valued significantly, which he says traditional models undervalue (JjeFktc4QLM [07:39]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's account is that a point late in a close game moves the final outcome more than a point in a decided game (JjeFktc4QLM [03:34]). The talk does not say where the 2% and 23% figures come from; how any model behind them was built and checked is not shown in the captions beyond the framework in [[framework--markov-decision-process-advantage-function-valuation]].

**When to apply** — When a number sums events across games with very different states (grades, loads, counting stats). Inference: for football, tag snaps as close or blowout by score margin and quarter and compare a player's grade with and without the blowout snaps before using it in a playing-time or recruiting decision. Eric's baseline: no direct position (method-baseline.md has none on player-valuation or leverage-weighted models).

# Valuing actions with a Markov decision process and an advantage function

**What it is** — The speaker, Ben Jenkins, frames basketball as a Markov decision process: a current state, an action taken, a stochastic transition, and an immediate reward measured both in expected points and in change in win probability (JjeFktc4QLM [04:05]). The key quantity is an advantage function: the expected value of an action beyond the baseline state expectation, which makes the valuation context-aware (JjeFktc4QLM [04:35]). Credit is split in two ways.
- **On-ball offense** (shots, assists, turnovers): valued by action type, player role and game context (JjeFktc4QLM [04:35], [05:07]).
- **Defense and off-ball influence**: valued by presence and constraints, not individual actions, to capture deterrence unseen in box scores (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07]).
The speaker positions it against three earlier families: box-score metrics (PER, win shares, box plus-minus: fixed weights, overweight scoring, weak on defense, no context), adjusted and regularized adjusted plus-minus (RAPM: regress possession outcomes on who is on the floor, but assume context-invariant contributions and miss synergy), and sequential models such as expected possession value (capture flow but struggle to credit players) (JjeFktc4QLM [01:01], [01:31], [02:02], [02:32]). The video description also names temporal-difference learning and a distributional win-probability model; the captions do not describe them. One caption spelling, "DRPM", appears for the model's name (JjeFktc4QLM [15:49]).

**Why it works** — The speaker says deep reinforcement learning can combine the strength of sequential models (context and the flow of play) with player-level credit (JjeFktc4QLM [02:02], [02:32]). The captions give no training details, so how well the learned values are calibrated is not stated.

**When to apply** — As a checklist for what a valuation model must handle: state, action, transition, reward, a baseline for "expected from this state", and a separate route for value that is not an action (defense, spacing). Inference: for football, ask the same questions of any grade or load number before comparing players. Eric's baseline: no direct position on valuation models (method-baseline.md).

**When NOT to apply** — Untested for this audience: the captions show no model specification, no calibration and no uncertainty for player values, and predictive accuracy is shown only on a chart (JjeFktc4QLM [11:42]). It was built on about five seasons of NBA play-by-play (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]); a football version needs its own state definition and a win-probability model, and none was shown. The defensive-value claims rest on the model with no independent check named.

**Example** — The speaker's own: a made three as the action, with reward measured as expected points on the play plus change in win probability (JjeFktc4QLM [04:05]).

**Related** — [[principle--identical-actions-carry-different-win-value-by-game-state]], [[framework--neural-shapley-credit-and-player-dropout]], [[claim--drl-shapley-predicts-games-better-than-box-metrics-but-not-vegas]].

# Splitting team value among players with neural Shapley values, and the portability objection

**What it is** — The attribution problem: ten players interact on the court, so a simple credit system ignores context and interaction (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07], [05:38]). The speaker, Ben Jenkins, uses Shapley values to allocate total team value among players. Each player is replaced with a baseline embedding learned from the reinforcement-learning model, and the change in expected points and win probability is measured; this also exposes synergy, meaning teammates who perform better or worse together (JjeFktc4QLM [06:08]). Exact Shapley values are computationally heavy, so a neural approximation is used (JjeFktc4QLM [06:08], [06:38]). In the Q&A a questioner (a judge) objects that the Shapley values are contextual, not designed to be portable across lineups, yet validation sums them to predict games (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [13:44], [14:16]). The speaker agrees ("I think you're right about that") and proposes player dropout: instead of using dropout for regularization, swap each player for a neutral baseline embedding, measure the change in win prediction, and sum over the five on the court (JjeFktc4QLM [14:16], [14:46]). He says this was not in the paper and he expects a better estimate. A second questioner describes the method as averaging a player "across all combinations with a guy out of the lineup" and asks about two players who "platoon all the time" (JjeFktc4QLM [15:18]); the speaker answers that the model accounts for who is on the court and that five seasons of play-by-play limits the sample problem, though new players need extrapolation that is "a little bit limited" in accuracy (JjeFktc4QLM [15:19], [15:49], [16:21]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's case is that the baseline-embedding swap prices each player against a neutral replacement. The "averages over who is present" description is the second questioner's wording (JjeFktc4QLM [15:18]), not a mechanism the speaker states. The captions give no further mechanism, and the judge's objection is that this contextual value is then used as if context-free.

**When to apply** — When you must split a unit's result among its members and the members interact (a five-man group, a pairing). Inference: the portability objection means a player's Shapley value is best read as value within the lineups he played in, not a transferable rating.

**When NOT to apply** — Contested inside the talk: the judge's objection and the speaker's partial concession (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [14:16]) leave the portability problem open, and the proposed dropout fix is not validated in the captions. A questioner raised that pairs who nearly always play together give few samples; the speaker replied that with five seasons of play-by-play "the sample size isn't necessarily a problem," except for new players, where extrapolation is "a little bit limited" (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]). Both the concern and the reply are unvalidated in the captions. Inference: in college football, with 11 players per side and yearly turnover, a five-player Shapley split needs many more shared snaps than the talk's NBA data had, and none were checked.

**Example** — Raised in the Q&A exchange (attribution unclear at the speaker change): Jokic and Murray, who are usually on the court together (caption spelling), as the hard case for attribution (JjeFktc4QLM [16:21]).

**What it is** — Ben Jenkins argues that winning is contextual: the same action has very different value depending on game state, teammates and opponents (JjeFktc4QLM [00:00], [00:31]). # Splitting team value among players with neural Shapley values, and the portability objection

-**What it is** — The attribution problem: ten players interact on the court, so a simple credit system ignores context and interaction (JjeFktc4QLM [05:07], [05:38]). The speaker, Ben Jenkins, uses Shapley values to allocate total team value among players. Each player is replaced with a baseline embedding learned from the reinforcement-learning model, and the change in expected points and win probability is measured; this also exposes synergy, meaning teammates who perform better or worse together (JjeFktc4QLM [06:08]). Exact Shapley values are computationally heavy, so a neural approximation is used (JjeFktc4QLM [06:08], [06:38]). In the Q&A a questioner (a judge) objects that the Shapley values are contextual, not designed to be portable across lineups, yet validation sums them to predict games (JjeFktc4QLM [13:13], [13:44], [14:16]). The speaker agrees ("I think you're right about that") and proposes player dropout: instead of using dropout for regularization, swap each player for a neutral baseline embedding, measure the change in win prediction, and sum over the five on the court (JjeFktc4QLM [14:16], [14:46]). He says this was not in the paper and he expects a better estimate. A second questioner describes the method as averaging a player "across all combinations with a guy out of the lineup" and asks about two players who "platoon all the time" (JjeFktc4QLM [15:18]); the speaker answers that the model accounts for who is on the court and that five seasons of play-by-play limits the sample problem, though new players need extrapolation that is "a little bit limited" in accuracy (JjeFktc4QLM [15:19], [15:49], [16:21]).

+1. **Baseline tags still missing.** About 20 of the 45 fixes added an Explicit tag to an interview or SportSmith quote, or the course-team, speaker-unconfirmed caveat to an Inferred HHPR line. One entry carried an inflated source ("transcript and slides" where the baseline says transcript only). The quotes themselves were verbatim.

+2. **Caption smoothing inside quotation marks, and garbles resolved to one reading.** Examples: "mirror"/"mere", "jumped"/"jump", "information gain"/"game", "catch up"/"ketchup", "20-yard shuttle", "two-thirds guessed 60", "velocity" from "Hardy through", and the [20:52] receivers/scheme line. A dropped hedge ("necessarily") belongs here too. No core number was invented.

+3. **Voice drift: pronouns and relationships the captions do not give.** "she/her" and "he/his" for speakers the captions never assign a pronoun (about 15 instances across the 40NV3_u9tYY and J7smyg1Czik talks). Relationships were also inferred: "same presenters", whose co-author someone is, a video narrator credited to the speaker, and a Q&A answer pinned on one of two presenters.
+4. **Smaller defects:**
+   - `supported` given to a second-hand survey (1 entry) or a method-only entry (1); `contested` with no real conflict (1).
+   - 3 locators one block off or wrong.
+   - Unlabelled synthesis in When NOT to apply and in Examples (4).
+## Persistence of earlier-round patterns (r0 to r3, read after the verdicts above)
+- **Baseline tags dropped** (r0 #1, r1 #1, r3 #1): **persists.** It was the largest category this round. The r1 to r3 sweep did not catch it, even though r0 and r3 both suggested a grep.
+- **Garbles flagged once, then smoothed** (r0 #2, r3 #2): **persists**, mostly in quotes.
+- **Q&A and attribution drift** (r2 #1, r3 #2): **persists in a narrower form.** Named-person attribution is now clean. Pronouns and person relationships are where it shows up now.

+- **`supported` given to second-hand or procedure-only data** (r1 #2, r3 #3): **mostly resolved.** Two cases remained and were lowered (surgery misperceptions; DeepQB model inputs, method only). The fatigue odds entry is borderline but keeps `supported` (case-control method with reported odds).
+- **Sibling cross-check** (r2 #2): **resolved.** The censor vs keep conflict is recorded as `contested`, and no new unflagged conflicts were found.
+## Reciprocal-link suggestions (not applied)
+- claim--faster-pitches-load-the-elbow-more <-> principle--throwing-harder-raises-risk-and-performance: neither links the other.
+- claim--youth-specialization-survey-and-early-surgery <-> claim--surgery-misperceptions-among-youth-players-and-parents: both mention draftees who had surgery before the draft.
+## Recommendation

+**Needs one more fix pass before promotion, then ready.** No NO-GO was found and no number was invented. The FIX edits are applied. The open risk is the out-of-scope half: the same three patterns (missing baseline tags, quote smoothing, pronouns) probably affect the other 72 entries. Before promoting, run this folder-wide grep and fix whatever it finds:
+- "Eric's baseline:" lines lacking Explicit, Inferred or Adopted
+- Inferred HHPR or course lines lacking "speaker unconfirmed"
+- `\b(he|she|his|her)\b` where the speaker is unnamed
+Then do a spot check of 10 entries, not a full round.

# The Women's Health Initiative: A Stopped Trial and a Later Reanalysis

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari") tells the Women's Health Initiative (WHI) story as an example of what assumptions and analysis choices can do (an7u-tVP5Xc [20:32] to [23:37]). The account, unverified here:
- **Scale:** 161,000 women took part, with a randomized controlled trial component of about 70,000, assigned to things like a low-fat diet or hormone replacement therapy (an7u-tVP5Xc [21:03] to [21:35]).
- **Regimen:** the hormone arm used an oral estrogen, conjugated equine estrogen in the caption, and "hydroxy progesterone" in the caption, where current practice uses 17 beta estradiol worn as a patch and micronized progesterone (an7u-tVP5Xc [21:35] to [22:06]). The caption spelling of the progesterone is likely garbled.
- **Stop:** the study was stopped by 2002 after strokes, clots, pulmonary emboli and cardiovascular events; prescriptions "plummeted" (an7u-tVP5Xc [22:06] to [22:36]).
- **Reanalysis:** in 2016 "they realized, oh, we analyzed the data wrong"; the problem was in women who started therapy over age 60 or more than 10 years past menopause (an7u-tVP5Xc [22:36]).
- **Consequence:** an entire generation of women was told to endure symptoms with nothing offered (an7u-tVP5Xc [22:36] to [23:07]).
- **The speaker's lessons:** be careful what goes to the media, "slice the data different ways," and repeat studies to confirm they reproduce (an7u-tVP5Xc [23:07] to [23:37]).

**Why it works** — The speaker notes that the regimens differ from what is used now (an7u-tVP5Xc [21:35] to [22:06]) and says the reanalysis located the problem in later starters (an7u-tVP5Xc [22:36]). The speaker gives no details of the reanalysis method. Inference: a pooled analysis of a mixed group can hide a subgroup difference, so splitting by a variable such as timing can reverse a conclusion; in sport data the analog would be pooling position groups or training ages.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a cautionary example when a single pooled result is about to change practice, to prompt slicing by plausible subgroups and waiting for replication. Eric's baseline: none; method-baseline.md contains nothing on hormone therapy or reanalysis.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: a single case told secondhand by a speaker whose subject is research quality, and the transcript cannot confirm any of the clinical or study details. Do not use it for clinical guidance on hormone therapy. Dates and the age and years-since-menopause cutoff are the speaker's statements. It involves older women and menopause, not collegiate athletes.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the same trial, first read as showing harm and a reason to avoid hormone therapy, then read as harm limited to women who started late (an7u-tVP5Xc [22:06] to [22:36]).

**Related** — [[framework--literature-audit-fields-for-female-athlete-research]] (a way to see how a study defined its population).
=================== claim--audit-results-female-participation-and-menstrual-reporting.md
confidence: untested

# Audit Numbers: Women in Sport Research and Menstrual Status Reporting

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari") reports figures from literature audits (method in the framework entry), plus one widely quoted figure whose origin she explains. Every number below is as spoken; the captions are auto-generated. Confidence is untested: the figures are summarized aloud with no n and no stated unit.
- **Top journals:** she calls the 6% "a number that has been thrown ... around a lot in the news" and explains where it comes from: in the top sports medicine and sports science journals from 2014 to 2020, "just looking at the top few," only 6% of articles focus solely on women (an7u-tVP5Xc [14:21]). She does not present it as her own group's audit result.
- **Supplement research:** 99.5% of supplement research did not categorize or standardize the menstrual cycle, even in studies of women (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:56]).
- **Two audit periods (2011 to 2013, then 2021 to 2023):** the captions say "39% female participants in studies" and, more recently, "44% um had female participants" (an7u-tVP5Xc [18:30]). The unit is unclear: it may be a share of studies with female participants or a share of participants who were female. Female-only studies "didn't improve all that much," going from 8.76 to 7.15; the unit is not stated and she says the female-only figure "declined" (an7u-tVP5Xc [18:30] to [19:00]). Male-only studies went from about 28% to 18.6 or 19% (an7u-tVP5Xc [19:00]).
- **Menstrual status reporting:** from not reported at all in 2011 to 2013 papers to about 5.6% of the recent papers (an7u-tVP5Xc [19:00]). On her gold, silver and bronze classification, 7% of those recent studies were silver and 0.5% gold, as captioned (an7u-tVP5Xc [19:00] to [19:30]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's interpretation is that overall female participation grew while female-only work did not, so "we have to do a better job" (an7u-tVP5Xc [19:00] to [19:30]). She gives no mechanism for the pattern. Inference: more studies enrolled women mainly as part of mixed samples, which would raise participation without raising female-specific work, but she does not say so.

**When to apply** — To ground a statement that menstrual status is rarely reported or standardized in sport research, with the limits below. Eric's baseline: none; method-baseline.md holds no position on female-athlete research quality. Inference: use the figures as a reason to check how any cited women's-sport study determined menstrual status.

**When NOT to apply** — The unit of the female-only figures is not stated and the audit topics and number of papers are not given (an7u-tVP5Xc [18:30]). The 99.5% is for supplement research specifically, not all sport research. The 6% is for the top few journals in 2014 to 2020, articles focusing solely on women. The audit figures are summarized aloud without published tables, and the 6% is a quoted figure, not shown to be from her audits. Do not present them as current for every topic. The speaker leads an institute that receives philanthropic funding (an7u-tVP5Xc [25:40]), and the talk offers no independent check of the audit method.

**Example** — From the audit: the share of recent papers reporting menstrual status at all was about 5.6%, up from none (an7u-tVP5Xc [19:00]).

**Related** — [[framework--literature-audit-fields-for-female-athlete-research]]. [[principle--asking-about-menstrual-status-is-not-testing-it]].
=================== claim--female-athlete-injury-risk-ratios-as-stated.md

# Stated Injury Ratios for Women Versus Men, With No Sources Given

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari") gives these incidence comparisons for female versus male athletes (an7u-tVP5Xc [06:40] to [07:10]):
- Concussion: 1.4 times greater in women than in men in comparable sports (an7u-tVP5Xc [06:40]).
- ACL tears: two to eight times greater risk in females (an7u-tVP5Xc [07:10]).
- Bone stress injuries: three times greater incidence (an7u-tVP5Xc [07:10]).
- Relative energy deficiency in sport: "very prevalent," from a full eating disorder to inadvertent under-fueling, and the speaker says much of it is societal, from pressure about how female athletes look and from their environments (an7u-tVP5Xc [07:10]).

The speaker also reports what Team USA athletes said they wanted researched: pregnancy and postpartum guidelines, menstrual cycle symptoms, effects of birth control, fueling across the cycle, mental health, recovery, and more women coaches (an7u-tVP5Xc [07:42] to [08:43]). The talk gives no sources, ranges or populations for any ratio.

**Why it works** — The speaker gives no mechanism for the ratios; the speaker presents them as context for why research is needed. Inference: the wide ACL range (two to eight times) suggests the figure depends heavily on the sport and the study, but the speaker does not discuss it.

**When to apply** — As a stated reason that women's programs need their own data, with the sources checked first. Eric's baseline: "We don't have any formal risk model that we follow." and screens: "there isn't anything that changes decisions made to a program; it's more or less just collected and referred to for future needs." (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q12). Inference: the ratios offer no screening method, so they create no conflict with that practice and add no new tool. Reciprocal-link suggestions (not compared in this batch): [[hewett-2006-anterior-cruciate-ligament-injuries-in-female-athletes]], [[collings-2026-an-evidence-based-and-mechanistic-approach-to-reducing-the-risk-of-anterior-cruciate-ligam]].

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: three bare ratios (plus an unquantified energy-deficiency statement) with no source, interval or sport, spoken aloud. They are group comparisons and say nothing about risk for an individual athlete. The range for ACL tears is wide. Do not quote these in a staff or athlete document without finding the underlying studies. Not guidance for football.

**Example** — The speaker's own list of the stated ratios above: concussion 1.4 times, ACL two to eight times, bone stress injuries three times (an7u-tVP5Xc [06:40] to [07:10]).

=================== claim--hormone-measurement-methods-and-their-limits.md
confidence: untested

# Four Ways to Measure Hormones, Four Sets of Limits

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari", introduced as director, co-founder and president of Women's Health and Sports Performance Institute) summarizes the limits of each sampling route, prompted by patients bringing printouts from a $1,000 blood test and a claim that a wearable "has been validated against these hormones" (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:17] to [31:47]). The speaker's questions for any such test: what assay was used, how was it tested, and how was the sample stored (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:47]).
- **Saliva:** cheap, but needs many measures on multiple days (frequent sampling), and validation is weaker because "those assays aren't that great yet" (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:47]).
- **Blood:** more expensive and involves a needle, so not done daily, but gives precise hormone quantification. Timing matters: the cycle phase at the draw, and hormones that differ morning versus afternoon (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:47] to [32:17]).
- **Dried blood spot:** you cannot check a thousand hormones from a spot "right now"; it needs repeated sampling and performs well with some moderate concentrations of certain hormones, with caution (an7u-tVP5Xc [32:17] to [32:48]).
- **Urine:** easy to collect and extensively validated against serum, but expensive to analyze every day; good as a profiling tool for patterns over a month or two, not exact concentrations (an7u-tVP5Xc [32:48]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives each limit as a stated trade-off and cites no studies; the claims are the speaker's clinical view. The talk does not give assay names, sensitivity or cost figures.

**When to apply** — As questions to ask when a vendor, athlete or coach proposes hormone-based monitoring for a women's team. Inference: route the decision to Athletic Medicine, which would own any hormone testing. Eric's baseline: "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." (Eric, interview 2026-09-28, Q23; Explicit.) Inference: so hormone sampling would be a new data stream outside current practice.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the table of limits is the speaker's assertion without citations or numbers. It is not a clinical guide to ordering tests. The statement about dried blood spots is made with a reference to Theranos and is a general caution, not a measurement result. The talk does not address which route fits athletes in a collegiate setting.

**Example** — The speaker's own: an athlete's $1,000 blood test printout that "checked all the things," which prompts the questions about assay, testing and storage (an7u-tVP5Xc [31:17] to [31:47]).

**Related** — [[principle--asking-about-menstrual-status-is-not-testing-it]]. [[framework--wearable-validation-workflow]] (hormones as the reference measure).

confidence: supported

# Audit the Female-Athlete Literature on Six Fields Before Trusting It

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari", a sports doctor and endocrinologist, an7u-tVP5Xc [13:21]) says the speaker's group and collaborators audit literature against set standards: pick a topic, find every paper with search terms, screen, then record (an7u-tVP5Xc [14:53] to [16:56]):
1. **Population:** men, women, biological females or males; how the population was defined and confirmed (an7u-tVP5Xc [15:23]).
2. **Athlete caliber:** tier 0 sedentary, tier 1 moving a little, tier 2 working out at least three times a week with the intention of competing at least once a year ("not a big step"), up to tier 5 world class. The speaker also asks whether the paper reports physical activity level at all (an7u-tVP5Xc [15:23] to [15:54]). The captions garble the tier 0 and tier 1 wording; tiers 3 and 4 are not described.
3. **Menstrual status:** how it was determined (an7u-tVP5Xc [15:54] to [16:25]); see the principle entry on asking versus testing.
4. **Research theme:** performance or health (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]).
5. **Study impact:** the journal's impact factor (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25] to [16:56]).
6. **Sample size:** "nine women or 9,000 women" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:56]).

Purpose: understand how well female athletes are represented, find performance level and menstrual status handling, highlight strengths and problems without "dissing" earlier work, mine past work for questions, and track trends across subdisciplines and time (an7u-tVP5Xc [17:27] to [17:58]). The audit was run on 2011 to 2013 papers and again on 2021 to 2023 papers (an7u-tVP5Xc [17:58] to [18:30]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is that studies often just say "women" or "men," so the fields force each paper to show who was studied and how (an7u-tVP5Xc [15:54]). The audit results the speaker reports from this method are in the claim entry on audit results.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a screening grid when a coach or athlete cites a study about a women's team, to see at once whether the participants resemble collegiate athletes (tier 2 and above), how menstrual status was determined, and how large the sample was. Inference: it can also be applied to the Zotero library for any women's-sport question. Eric's baseline: none; method-baseline.md states no rule for appraising outside studies.

**When NOT to apply** — The caliber tiers are described only partly in the transcript, so a tier-by-tier coding needs the published scheme (not in the talk). The audit topic coverage and number of papers are not stated. The fields describe reporting quality, not whether a result is true. Not designed for male or mixed-sex football studies, though the population and sample-size fields transfer.

**Example** — The speaker's own: the finding that 99.5% of supplement studies did not categorize or standardize menstrual cycle was reported as an audit result (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:56]); the captions do not say which field produced it (Inference: field 3, menstrual status). Inference: a paper that says only "women" without caliber or menstrual status would have gaps in fields 2 and 3.

**Related** — [[claim--audit-results-female-participation-and-menstrual-reporting]] (what the audit found). [[principle--asking-about-menstrual-status-is-not-testing-it]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[moore-2024-menstrual-cycle-phasebased-strength-conditioning-training-for-elite-team-sport-female-athl]] (not compared in this batch).

confidence: untested

# A Wearable Validation Workflow: Question, Prepare, Validate, Reproduce, Then Share

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari") lays out a decision flow for using wearable data in research (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19] to [34:22]):
1. **Start with the research question.** Are the data appropriate for it, and is it a high-impact question? If not, "back to the drawing board" (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19]).
2. **Prepare the data:** address sensor accuracy, missing data and outliers (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19] to [33:51]).
3. **Validate** the wearable against something you can trust, in her example hormone measures, using a survey that gives baseline information about the wearer and a diverse group of users (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:19] to [33:51]).
4. **Reproduce known values or trends.** If not, look again. If yes, analyze (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:51]).
5. **Check for robust conclusions** that answer the question. If yes, share. If not, you learn what is missing and can refine the question and the prospective data collection (an7u-tVP5Xc [33:51] to [34:22]).

Her wider advice: use multiple wearables, validate against hormones, tweak the wearable, and ask questions over time (an7u-tVP5Xc [34:22]). Run it as a team: an endocrinologist, a sports physician, athlete input and a data analytics expert (an7u-tVP5Xc [29:14], [34:53] to [35:24]).

Background reasons she gives: sensors differ in what they measure and in validity, so "any wearable" data are "apples and oranges"; with no test against a gold standard "we're making a lot of assumptions" (an7u-tVP5Xc [20:32], [28:44] to [29:14]). She also raises data quality, health equity, algorithm bias, privacy and AI repeating errors with more confidence (an7u-tVP5Xc [29:44] to [31:17]).

**Why it works** — The speaker's reason is the validity point above: unvalidated devices carry unexamined assumptions. She gives no study showing the workflow itself improves results. Inference: the loop of step 5 treats a failed validation as information, not a wasted study.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a one-page checklist before adopting any consumer wearable, sleep or cycle-tracking product with a women's team, asking whether the device was validated against a trusted standard and in athletes like Baylor's. Eric's baseline: modified reactive strength index from daily CMJ replaced subjective wellness surveys because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-19). Eric's baseline: "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-20). Inference: the talk agrees with preferring validated, consistent measures and adds a validation step before adoption.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: this is the speaker's flow, shown without a worked example or outcomes. Her reference standard is hormone testing for cycle-related wearables; other devices need their own trusted reference. It is a research workflow, not a procurement standard, and it does not say how much validation is enough. Her view that a team is needed is an institutional opinion; she leads an institute with philanthropic funding (an7u-tVP5Xc [25:40]).

**Example** — The speaker's own: a person who says "just plug in your wearable data," and her reply, "which wearable?" (an7u-tVP5Xc [28:44]).

**Related** — [[claim--hormone-measurement-methods-and-their-limits]] (the reference measures). [[heuristic--survey-strengths-and-weaknesses-for-athlete-research]]. Reciprocal-link suggestion: [[framework--evidence-stacking-before-acting]] in the Old Bull library (combining independent evidence before acting).
=================== heuristic--survey-strengths-and-weaknesses-for-athlete-research.md
confidence: untested

# Use Surveys for Prevalence and Early Ideas, Not Cause

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari") says "you've got to start with surveys," but to be careful how they are built (an7u-tVP5Xc [27:41]).
- **Strengths:** cheap, early dissemination, large cohorts, assess prevalence, and results can show correlations that inspire later investigation (an7u-tVP5Xc [27:41] to [28:12]).
- **Weaknesses:** cross-sectional so no causal conclusion; selection bias; recall bias; non-response bias (an7u-tVP5Xc [28:12]).

Where it sits in the speaker's research approach: audit the literature, then observational, correlational and prevalence studies, then intervention studies, then repeat the findings, then advocacy and education; the speaker says it takes about 17 years from discovering something to common practice (an7u-tVP5Xc [26:40] to [27:41]). The 17-year figure is given without a source.

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the strengths and weaknesses as a list and no mechanism. Inference: surveys suit early stages because they are cheap and wide, and their listed biases are why they cannot carry the later, causal stages.

**When to apply** — Inference: as the critique list for any staff survey of women athletes, and for judging how much weight a survey result deserves. Eric's baseline: daily subjective wellness surveys, rolled out from summer 2022, were dropped after about one academic year because athletes learned to game the consistent, low-effort answers, and they are kept for return-to-play and chronic health conditions (Explicit, SportSmith article 2026-02-19). Inference: the talk extends that with named bias types and still values surveys for prevalence and early ideas; it does not mention athletes gaming answers.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: the list is the speaker's own, with no citation. A brief talk segment, not a methods guide. It does not cover how to build a good survey. For monitoring a team daily, Eric's baseline experience (above) is a repeated-measure problem the list does not address.

**Example** — The speaker's own: surveys "assess prevalence" and can inspire future investigations, but being cross-sectional they cannot establish cause (an7u-tVP5Xc [27:41] to [28:12]).

**Related** — [[framework--wearable-validation-workflow]]. [[framework--literature-audit-fields-for-female-athlete-research]] (step one of the same research approach).
=================== principle--asking-about-menstrual-status-is-not-testing-it.md
confidence: untested

# Asking About Menstrual Status Is Not the Same as Testing It

**What it is** — The speaker (caption spelling "Kate Ari," a sports doctor and endocrinologist) makes a measurement-validity point: asking someone about their cycle is "not the same as actually testing the hormone levels" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). Someone on a birth control pill who reports a period has a withdrawal bleed while taking exogenous hormones, "not the same as having a natural menstrual cycle" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). She asks researchers to use the same terminology: a withdrawal bleed from a pill, a naturally menstruating woman, and someone who ovulated and has a normal cycle are "all very different things" (an7u-tVP5Xc [20:01] to [20:32]). On her audit's gold, silver and bronze classification, she says gold and silver are where studies did some hormonal measurement and also reported and asked about status (an7u-tVP5Xc [19:00] to [19:30]); bronze is not defined in the transcript.

She also says it is not known whether training should change by cycle phase: "we don't know when it matters because we're not studying it enough," and it may be that nothing needs to change in someone without symptoms (an7u-tVP5Xc [08:43] to [09:14]).

**Why it works** — The speaker gives the definitional reasons above and no data. Inference: grouping athletes by self-reported phase mixes people with different hormonal states, which would blur any phase comparison, but she does not run this through.

**When to apply** — Inference: before any internal analysis groups women athletes by cycle phase, record how status was determined (asked, hormone-tested, or on a pill with a withdrawal bleed). Inference: Athletic Medicine and Performance Nutrition would own the health data. Eric's baseline: Performance Nutrition is a separate unit that owns body composition and fueling (Explicit, Playbook p.5), and no force-plate or GPS data flow to it proactively (Explicit, interview 2026-09-28, Q24). Inference: so who records cycle information and where it is stored would need agreeing between those units.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is untested: these are definitions and an expert's position, with no data or citations in the talk. It gives no training recommendation by phase; she says the evidence is missing (an7u-tVP5Xc [08:43]). It does not say how often hormone testing is needed or practical for a team. It is not a clinical guide for any individual.

**Example** — The speaker's own: an athlete says "I'm on my period" while taking a birth control pill; that is a withdrawal bleed on exogenous hormones, "not the same as having a natural menstrual cycle" (an7u-tVP5Xc [16:25]). Inference: a study coding her as in a natural cycle phase would misclassify her.

**Related** — [[claim--audit-results-female-participation-and-menstrual-reporting]]. [[claim--hormone-measurement-methods-and-their-limits]]. # Review R=0: 42 Analytics SSAC entries (12-entry sample)
Sample: `ls | grep -v '^_' | sort | awk 'NR%3==0' | awk 'NR%4==0'` gave 12 files. I read every cited window in each `transcript.md` and checked baseline lines against `docs/method-baseline.md`.
## Cross-entry patterns
1. **Baseline tags dropped or misplaced.** Three entries quote Explicit baseline lines without the tag, and one puts a baseline fact inside "Inference:". Grep the folder for "Eric's baseline" lines that lack "Explicit" or "Inferred".
2. **Caption garbles flagged once, then smoothed.** Entries flag one garble and clean the next ("about 35", "th000" at [20:24], "assisted three rates"). Every garbled number needs its own flag.
3. **Unlabelled connective claims.** Plausible links are written as the speaker's statements ("his own win-probability model", "sensors recorded linear acceleration only", "of which two players", "the questioner sums it up"). These are exactly the unlabelled claims the brief bans.
Dedup: I found no restatements within the folder. I grepped the SecondBrain library for elbow, concussion, pitch count, SHAP, cluster analysis, placebo, win probability, stress tolerance, benchmark and leverage. The hits are unrelated uses (joint mechanics, Myszka constraints) or research-paper briefs that the entries already link (Carey 2017). No NO-GO: every number I checked is in the transcript at or next to its locator.
## Verdict
**GO AFTER FIXES.** 3 GO, 9 FIX, 0 NO-GO. All fixes are text-level. One confidence change is recommended: the soccer entry from supported to untested.
######## review_42analytics_r1.md
# Review: 42 Analytics SSAC entries, sample R=1 (13 entries)
Reviewer: R1, 2026-10-01. Read-only. Every locator below was checked against `transcript.md`. Eric's baseline quotes were checked in `docs/method-baseline.md`.
## Cross-entry patterns
1. **Eric's-baseline tags dropped.** Five entries quote Eric's interview without the **Explicit** tag (the CLIP case study, defensive three-point percentage, chemistry, player credit, and the Q3 and Q2a quotes generally). The Inferred tags were kept correctly (chronotype, familiarity). Quotes are sometimes pulled from an unrelated topic (ACWR used for player credit, Q3 used for CLIP film review).
2. **`supported` given to procedures or second-hand reports.** Of five `supported` entries in this sample, two describe a procedure with no cited result (injury coding) or relay an uncited study (chronotype). A third mixes a real study with bare assertions (UCL cost). Scope each rating, or downgrade it.
3. **Small attribution drift.** The atomizer paraphrases past the transcript: "private", "advises a motion-capture company", "she, a sleep scientist", a counterfactual rationale never stated, and "not really a thing" credited to the speaker alone. Several locators sit one 30-second block late. None is fabricated, but each states more than the captions say.
No duplicates. The familiarity claim's carry-over sentence overlaps `claim--familiarity-gains-diminish-across-seasons` but serves a different purpose. The injury-coding entry complements `framework--checklist-for-reading-load-and-injury-papers`. No vault overlap was found (grep: chronotype, nap, Tommy John/UCL, tanking, Capology, three-point). Every Related link resolves.
## Overall verdict (sample R=1)
**GO AFTER FIXES.** GO 1, FIX 12, NO-GO 0. No invented numbers. Every When NOT to apply section is present and specific. The fixes are confidence scoping (4 entries), one misread data description (familiarity 1600 / 2023-24), one misread finding (position effect), and the label and tag hygiene above.

# Review: 42 Analytics SSAC entries, sample R=2
The sample is 13 entries. Every locator below was read in `transcript.md`, and every "Eric's baseline" line was checked against `docs/method-baseline.md`.
## Cross-entry patterns
1. **Q&A attribution goes beyond the captions.** Entries pin lines on "the same speaker" or "the speaker's own", or name Luke, without speaker labels to support it. A questioner's wording is also treated as the speaker's mechanism.
2. **Sibling entries were not cross-checked.** The censor-versus-keep conflict (TbYgc6_qQzo vs TIRINmtZOu0) went unflagged, and two figures were called unreconciled when simple arithmetic reconciles them. Grep the folder before setting confidence.
3. **Framing around correct numbers.** The 6% was made the speaker's own audit, participants became papers, a garbled 25% became a yardage split, and "no sample size" was written over a stated 1,000 plays. No core number was mistranscribed.
## Verdict
**GO AFTER FIXES**: 5 GO, 8 FIX, 0 NO-GO. Nothing is invented. Every "Eric's baseline" line is verified and keeps its tag. The fixes are attribution, scoping and unlabelled sentences. One entry moves to `contested`, and two need their `supported` rating scoped.

Sample (12 entries): `ls | grep -v '^_' | sort | awk 'NR%3==0' | awk 'NR%4==3'`. Each entry's locators were checked against `transcript.md`, Eric's baseline lines against `docs/method-baseline.md`, and duplicates against this folder and the SecondBrain library.

## Cross-entry patterns
1. **Baseline tags dropped.** Three entries (clip, lineman, pressure-score) quote method-baseline.md but leave out the **Explicit** tag and replace it with a loose source description. A grep for `Eric's baseline:` lines missing "Explicit" or "Inferred" would catch this across the whole folder.
2. **Voice drift at the edges of the talk.** Q&A content gets reassigned or reversed: the questioner's reasoning given to the presenters (plan-rest), the speaker's Q&A position inverted (sleep), an ambiguous slide referent pinned on the speaker's own group (UCL). Captions also get smoothed into cleaner wording ("unspoken bond", "out of the pocket"). Q&A and garbled lines need the same quote-level check as the main talk.
3. **`supported` given to single-site or second-hand descriptive data.** Lineman (one team, no n, no outcome) and sleep (uncited second-hand studies, time in bed only) do not meet "method with results the entry cites" once their own When NOT sections are read. content.text:
Round 2 is done for my 11 talks (72 entries). I recommend promoting them once someone has skimmed the 30 edited files in `git diff`. There are no NO-GOs and no invented numbers.

**Counts:** 42 GO, 30 FIX, 0 NO-GO. That means 42% needed changes, and I've made all 30 edits in the entry files. Three confidence ratings changed:
- The Q3i3 charted-grades framework went from `supported` to `untested`.
- The JHge prediction-vs-attribution principle went from `untested` to `contested`, matching its twin entry.
- The 1nt8 pipeline stays `supported`, but only for stages 1 and 2.

**Top 3 recurring defects:**
1. **Caption garbles smoothed or misread (7 entries).** The worst case turned "tie dance in line tight ends" into "defensive line". Others reversed a garbled sentence's meaning, wrote "Fon score" as F1, and printed corrected names while calling them caption spellings.
2. **Q&A attribution and order drift (6 entries).** A questioner's remark was given to the presenter (K5a7). A Q&A exchange was put in the wrong order (Q3i3, the 0.75). A garbled answer was over-read in two pass-rush entries.
3. **Unlabelled additions (9 entries).** Examples: "run-heavy team", wages "spent", "2020-21" taken from the video description, "an athlete's" blood-test printout.

A fourth pattern: Ben Jenkins gave three of these talks, and his near-duplicate SSAC25/SSAC26 principles, validation entries and frameworks didn't link to each other. They're now linked both ways.

All three of these patterns were flagged in r0–r3 and still show up, mostly in Q&A and in sentences that cite another talk.

**Before merging:**
- Two entries I edited also cite EeBgUCYhezc, and the r4a reviewer was editing at the same time. Check those two for collisions.
- `_book.md`'s confidence tally is now out of date. I left it alone as instructed.
- Someone should decide whether to merge the two Jenkins principles or keep both with the link.
